metadata.title: A convex polyhedron without Rupert's property

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 1 (thm:main) is Section 7, a description of a computer-generated solution tree and its SageMath verification; extracted as one prose proof node spanning the whole section (subsections as steps), with the recursive exclusion scheme (I)-(III) as a nested algorithm.

The 2017 question of Jerrard-Wetzel-Yuan is phrased as a question but called a conjecture by the paper; typed conjecture (external) with a resolves edge to Theorem 1. The same sentence also states that Platonic solids are Rupert, which could not be split off.
Two prose observations motivating the Global Theorem are kept as claims; ClP8 is a weaker version of the Global Theorem and is linked by a generalizes edge.
The design desiderata list (1)-(4) and the narrative of how the Noperthedron was found (Section 9.1) were not extracted, as were computational statistics on the solution tree outside the proof.

nodes.name: Prince Rupert's cube (Wallis)
nodes.statement: In \cite[pp. 470]{Wallis1685} John Wallis proved a prediction by Prince Rupert of the Rhine concerning an interesting property of the three-dimensional cube: It is possible to cut a hole inside this solid such that an identical cube can pass through this hole.
nodes.statement_short: Wallis proved Prince Rupert's prediction that a hole can be cut through a cube so that an identical cube passes through it.
conclusions: It is possible to cut a hole inside this solid such that an identical cube can pass through this hole

nodes.name: Rupert conjecture (all convex polyhedra are Rupert)
nodes.statement: For instance, in \cite{Scriba68, JeWeYu17} it is proven that all Platonic solids are \emph{Rupert}, and the authors of \cite{JeWeYu17} asked whether all convex polyhedra in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have this property.
nodes.statement_short: All Platonic solids are Rupert; Jerrard-Wetzel-Yuan asked whether every convex polyhedron in R^3 is Rupert.
conclusions: all convex polyhedra in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have this property

nodes.name: Noperthedron is not Rupert
nodes.statement: The Noperthedron does not have Rupert's property.
conclusions: The Noperthedron does not have Rupert's property.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Polyhedron
nodes.statement: In this paper a \emph{polyhedron}, usually denoted by $\mathbf{P}$, is a finite non-degenerate set of points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ in convex position.
nodes.genus: finite non-degenerate set of points in $\mathbb{R}^3$

nodes.name: Convex hull and interior of a polyhedron
nodes.statement:
We will denote by $\overline{\mathbf{P}} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ the smallest convex set containing all points of a polyhedron $\mathbf{P}$ (i.e. including its interior)
and by $\mathbf{P}^\circ$ the interior of $\overline{\mathbf{P}}$.

nodes.name: Point-symmetric polyhedron
nodes.statement: Further, a polyhedron $\mathbf{P}$ is called point-symmetric (with respect to the origin) if $\mathbf{P} = -\mathbf{P}$, i.e. $-P \in \mathbf{P}$ for all $P \in \mathbf{P}$.

nodes.name: Radius of a polyhedron
nodes.statement: We will say that such a polyhedron $\mathbf{P}$ has radius $\rho > 0$ if for all $P \in \mathbf{P}$ it holds that $\|P\| \leq \rho$ and for some $P \in \mathbf{P}$ equality~holds.

nodes.name: Polygon
nodes.statement: A polygon, usually denoted by $\mathcal{P}$ or $\mathcal{Q}$, is a finite set of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that not all lie on the same line.
differentia: not all lie on the same line

nodes.name: Convex hull and interior of a polygon
nodes.statement: Similar to polyhedra, we denote by $\overline{\mathcal{P}}$ the convex hull of $\mathcal{P}$ and by $\mathcal{P}^\circ$ the interior of~ $\overline{\mathcal{P}}$.

nodes.name: Rotation matrix R, sphere parametrization X and projection M
nodes.statement_short: Defines the 2D rotation $R(\alpha)$, the unit-sphere parametrization $X(\theta,\varphi)$ and the orthogonal projection $M(\theta,\varphi)$ along $X$.
nodes.label: def:RXM

nodes.name: Action of R and M on point sets
nodes.statement: We let $R(\alpha)$ and $M(\theta,\varphi)$ act on \emph{sets of points} so that $R(\alpha) \mathcal{P}$ is a rotation of a polygon $\mathcal{P}$ and $M(\theta,\varphi) \mathbf{P}$ is a projection of a polyhedron $\mathbf{P}$.

nodes.name: Equivalent formulation of Rupert's property for point-symmetric polyhedra
nodes.statement: In \cite[Prop. 2]{StYu23} the following property is proven to be equivalent to the original statement of Rupert's property for pointsymmetric polyhedra.
nodes.statement_short: For point-symmetric polyhedra, the projection-inclusion condition is equivalent to the original Rupert's property.
conclusions: the following property is proven to be equivalent to the original statement of Rupert's property

nodes.name: Rupert's property
nodes.statement_short: P is Rupert if some rotated projection of P fits strictly inside the interior of another projection of P.
nodes.label: def:rupert

nodes.name: Rupert's condition
nodes.statement: R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P})^\circ.
nodes.label: eq:rupert_condition

nodes.name: Lipschitz-type bounds for M and RM
nodes.statement: \| M(\theta, \varphi) - M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) \| \leq \sqrt{2}\varepsilon \quad \text{and} \quad    \| R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi) - R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) \| \leq \sqrt{5} \varepsilon
nodes.statement_short: Projection matrices move by at most $\sqrt2\varepsilon$, rotated projections by at most $\sqrt5\varepsilon$, under $\varepsilon$-perturbations.
nodes.label: eq:sqrt2sqrt5intro

nodes.name: Solution space I
nodes.statement_short: The five-dimensional parameter space $I$ of Rupert's condition, to be partitioned into small regions each excluded.

nodes.name: Filled 5-dimensional cube notation
nodes.statement: For $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ we denote by $[\overline{\theta}_1 \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\varphi}_1 \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\theta}_2\pm \varepsilon, \overline{\varphi}_2\pm \varepsilon, \overline{\alpha} \pm \varepsilon]$ the \emph{filled} (closed) 5-dimensional cube with midpoint $(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ and side length $2 \varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Rotation matrices about the coordinate axes
nodes.statement:
We define the functions $R_x,R_y,R_z:$  $\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ by
    \[
            R_x(\alpha)\coloneqq 
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            1 & 0 & 0\\ 
            0 & \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha\\
            0 & \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha
        \end{pmatrix}, 
        \hspace{1cm}
        R_y(\alpha)\coloneqq 
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            \cos\alpha & 0 & -\sin\alpha\\ 
            0 & 1 & 0\\
            \sin\alpha & 0 & \cos\alpha
        \end{pmatrix},
    \]
    \[
        R_z(\alpha)\coloneqq 
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha &0\\
            \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha &0\\
            0 & 0 & 1
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \]
nodes.label: def:rotation

nodes.name: Additivity of axis rotations
nodes.statement: Note that since these matrices are simply rotations one has $R_a(\alpha)R_a(\beta)=R_a(\alpha+\beta)$ for $a \in \{x,y,z\}$.

nodes.name: Cyclic group C30
nodes.statement:
We define a representation of the cyclic group $\mathcal{C}_{30}$ by
\[
    \mathcal{C}_{30} \coloneqq \left\{(-1)^\ell R_z\left(\frac{2\pi k}{15}\right) \colon k=0,\dots,14; \ell=0,1\right\}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{C}_{30}$: the 30 matrices $\pm R_z(2\pi k/15)$.

nodes.name: Orbit under C30
nodes.statement: Note that $|\mathcal{C}_{30}| = 30$ and we will write $\mathcal{C}_{30} \cdot P = \{c P \,\text{ for } \, c \in \mathcal{C}_{30}\}$ for the orbit of $P$ under the action of $\mathcal{C}_{30}$.

nodes.name: Generator points C1, C2, C3
nodes.statement_short: Three explicit rational generator points in $\mathbb{Q}^3$.

nodes.name: Norms of the generator points
nodes.statement: Note that the distance from $C_1$ to the origin is exactly 1, and that $\frac{98}{100} < \|C_i\| < \frac{99}{100}$ for $i=2,3$.
conclusions: the distance from $C_1$ to the origin is exactly 1

nodes.name: Noperthedron
nodes.statement:
We define the set of points $\mathbf{NOP} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ by the action of $\mathcal{C}_{30}$ on $C_1,C_2,C_3$: 
    \[
        \mathbf{NOP} \coloneqq \mathcal{C}_{30} \cdot C_1 \cup \mathcal{C}_{30}\cdot C_2\cup \mathcal{C}_{30} \cdot C_3,
    \]
    and we call the resulting polyhedron the \emph{Noperthedron}.
nodes.statement_short: NOP is the union of the $\mathcal{C}_{30}$-orbits of $C_1,C_2,C_3$.

nodes.name: Noperthedron has 90 vertices
nodes.statement: Clearly, the \emph{Noperthedron} has $3 \cdot 30=90$ vertices.

nodes.name: Noperthedron is point-symmetric
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $-\mathrm{Id} = (-1)\cdot R_z(0) \in \mathcal{C}_{30}$, $\mathbf{NOP}$ is pointsymmetric with respect to the origin.
conclusions: $\mathbf{NOP}$ is pointsymmetric with respect to the origin

nodes.name: Vertex norms of the Noperthedron
nodes.statement: Finally, all vertices of $\mathbf{NOP}$ have Euclidean norm at most $1$ and at least ${98}/{100}$.
conclusions: all vertices of $\mathbf{NOP}$ have Euclidean norm at most $1$ and at least ${98}/{100}$

nodes.statement: For doing so, when $M \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times 3}$ (for $k \in \{2,3\}$) is a matrix and $\mathbf{P} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{3}$ a polyhedron (i.e. a set of points in $\mathbb{R}^3$), we will use the natural notation $M \cdot \mathbf{P}$ for the set of points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ given by $\{M \cdot P \text{ for } P \in \mathbf{P}\}$.

nodes.name: Symmetries of the Noperthedron projections
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron
nodes.statement_short: Projections of NOP are invariant under $\theta\mapsto\theta+2\pi/15$, $\alpha\mapsto\alpha+\pi$, and a reflection relates $\varphi$ to $\pi-\varphi$.
nodes.label: lem:symmetries

nodes.name: Proof of the symmetry lemma
nodes.statement:
The first two statements follow directly from the definition of $\mathcal{C}_{30}$, the identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR2}) above and the pointsymmetry of $\mathbf{P}$. The third identity can be checked with a simple computation using~that
    \[
        \begin{pmatrix}
            1 & 0\\
            0 & -1
        \end{pmatrix} \cdot 
        M(\theta, \varphi) = - M(\theta + \pi/15, \pi - \varphi) \cdot R_z(16 \pi/15),
    \]
    and that $- R_z(16 \pi/15) P \in \mathbf{P}$ if $P \in \mathbf{P}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron
nodes.statement_short: Direct verification from the definition of $\mathcal{C}_{30}$, identity (XMRfromR2), and point symmetry.

nodes.name: Reduced parameter intervals for NOP
nodes.statement:
If $\mathbf{NOP}$ is Rupert, then there exists a solution to its Rupert's condition (\ref{eq:rupert_condition}) with  
\begin{align*}    
\theta_1,\theta_2&\in[0,2\pi/15] \subset [0,0.42], \\
\varphi_1&\in [0,\pi] \subset [0,3.15],\\
\varphi_2&\in [0,\pi/2] \subset [0,1.58],\\
\alpha &\in [-\pi/2,\pi/2] \subset [-1.58,1.58].
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron
nodes.statement_short: If NOP is Rupert, a solution exists with $\theta_i\in[0,2\pi/15]$, $\varphi_2\in[0,\pi/2]$, $\alpha\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
conclusions:
there exists a solution to its Rupert's condition (\ref{eq:rupert_condition}) with  
\begin{align*}    
\theta_1,\theta_2&\in[0,2\pi/15] \subset [0,0.42], \\
\varphi_1&\in [0,\pi] \subset [0,3.15],\\
\varphi_2&\in [0,\pi/2] \subset [0,1.58],\\
\alpha &\in [-\pi/2,\pi/2] \subset [-1.58,1.58].
\end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:NOPbounds

nodes.name: Proof of reduced parameter intervals
nodes.statement:
Let us assume a solution $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha)$ to the Rupert condition
    $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P})^\circ$
    is given. Then, this inclusion still holds true, when mirroring all the points along the $x$-axis, hence
    $$\begin{pmatrix} 
        1&0\\
        0&-1
    \end{pmatrix}
    R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset \begin{pmatrix} 
        1&0\\
        0&-1
    \end{pmatrix}(M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P})^\circ.$$
    Using 
    \[
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            1&0\\
            0&-1
        \end{pmatrix}R(\alpha)=
        R({-\alpha})\begin{pmatrix} 
            1&0\\
            0&-1
        \end{pmatrix}
    \]
    and the third identity in \cref{lem:symmetries}, we arrive at
    \[
        R({-\alpha})M({\theta_1+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_1}) \mathbf{P}
        \subset (M({\theta_2+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_2})\mathbf{P})^\circ.
    \]
    So, if $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha)$ is a solution to Rupert's condition for $\mathbf{P}$, then 
    \[
        (\theta_1+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_1,\theta_2+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_2,-\alpha)
    \]
    is also a solution. It follows that we may assume that there exists a solution with $\varphi_2\in[0,\pi/2]$. Finally, using the first and second identity of \cref{lem:symmetries}, we can enforce the remaining parameters to lie in the claimed intervals.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron
nodes.statement_short: Mirror a solution and apply the third symmetry to get $\varphi_2\le\pi/2$, then use the other symmetries to reduce $\theta_i$ and $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Operator norm
nodes.statement: For a matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ we will write $\|A\|$ for its (operator) norm given by $\|A\| = \max_{v\in \mathbb{R}^n}\|Av\|/\|v\|$, where $\|v\|$ for vectors $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ denotes the usual Euclidean norm, as before.

nodes.name: Sub-multiplicativity and orthogonal invariance of the operator norm
nodes.statement: Recall that $\|.\|$ is sub-multiplicative and that multiplication by an orthogonal matrix (a matrix $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, such that $QQ^t = \mathrm{Id}$) leaves the norm unchanged.

nodes.name: Rotation and projection matrices have unit norm
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha, \theta,\varphi \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a \in \{x,y,z\}$ one has $\| R(\alpha)\| = \| R_a(\alpha)\| =\| M(\theta, \varphi)\| = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:RaRalpha

nodes.name: Proof of unit norms
nodes.statement: The statement is obvious for $R(\alpha), R_x(\alpha), R_y(\alpha), R_z(\alpha)$ since these matrices describe rotations. Identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR2}) shows that $\| M(\theta, \varphi)\| \leq 1$ by sub-multiplicativity, and it is easy to check that for the unit vector $v = (-\sin(\theta), \cos(\theta),0)^t$ it holds that $\|M(\theta, \varphi) v\| = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotations are orthogonal; for $M$ use identity (XMRfromR2) and a unit vector attaining norm 1.

nodes.name: Rotation difference bound
nodes.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$, $|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\leq\varepsilon$ and $a \in \{x,y,z\}$ then
$\|R_a(\alpha)-R_a({\overline{\alpha}})\|=\|R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha})\| < \varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:RaRa

nodes.name: Proof of rotation difference bound
nodes.statement:
We show the equality for $a=x$ only; so we calculate 
    \begin{align*}
        \|R_x(\alpha)-R_x({\overline{\alpha}})\| &= \max_{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2=1}\left\|
    \begin{pmatrix} 
        0 & 0 & 0\\ 
        0 & \cos(\alpha)-\cos(\overline{\alpha}) & -\sin(\alpha)+\sin(\overline{\alpha})\\
        0 & \sin(\alpha)-\sin(\overline{\alpha}) & \cos(\alpha)-\cos(\overline{\alpha})
    \end{pmatrix} 
    \begin{pmatrix} 
        v_1\\
        v_2\\
        v_3
    \end{pmatrix}\right\|\\
    &=\max_{v_2^2+v_3^2=1}\left\|\left(R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha})\right)\begin{pmatrix} 
        v_2\\
        v_3
    \end{pmatrix}\right\|\\
    &=\|R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha})\|.
    \end{align*}
    For the inequality we first observe that for any $v\in\mathbb{R}^2$ the points $R(\alpha)v$ and $R(\overline{\alpha})v$ lie on the circle with radius $\|v\|$. The length of the arc connecting them has length at most $|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\cdot \|v\|$ and is always longer than the straight line connecting them with length $\|R(\alpha)v-R(\overline{\alpha})v\|$. Hence we~have  
    \[
        \|R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha})\|=\max_{v\in\mathbb{R}^2} \frac{\|(R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha}))v\|}{\|v\|} < \max_{v\in\mathbb{R}^2} \frac{|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\cdot \|v\|}{\|v\|}=|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\leq \varepsilon. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $R_x$ to the 2D rotation, then compare chord and arc length on a circle.

nodes.name: Jensen-type cosine inequality
nodes.statement:
For all $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|a|,|b|\leq 2$ the following inequality holds:
    \[
        (1+\cos(a))(1+\cos(b))\geq 2+2\cos\Big(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\Big),
    \]
    with equality only for $a=0$ or $b=0$.
nodes.statement_short: $(1+\cos a)(1+\cos b)\ge 2+2\cos\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ for $|a|,|b|\le2$.
nodes.label: lem:jensen

nodes.name: Proof of Jensen-type cosine inequality
nodes.statement:
Using $1+ \cos(x) = 2 \cos(x/2)^2$ three times the inequality becomes equivalent to 
    \[
        \cos(a/2)^2 \cos(b/2)^2 \geq \cos(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}/2)^2.
    \]
    Note that without loss of generality we can assume that $0 \leq a, b \leq 2$; let $x=a/2$ and $y=b/2$ so that $0 \leq x,y\leq 1$. Then we need to prove that 
    \[
        \cos(x) \cos(y) \geq \cos(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}),
    \]
    Or, equivalently, 
    \[
        \frac{\cos(x+y) + \cos(x-y)}{2} \geq \cos(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}),
    \]
    as $2 \cos(x) \cos(y) = \cos(x+y) + \cos(x-y)$.
    Now the crucial observation is that $f(t) \coloneqq \cos(\sqrt{t})$ is \emph{convex} for $t \in [0,4]$. Indeed, 
    \[
        f''(t) = \frac{\sin(\sqrt{t}) - \sqrt{t} \cos(\sqrt{t})}{4 \sqrt{t^3}},
    \]
    and $f''(t) \geq 0$ on $t \in [0,4]$ is equivalent to $\sin(s) - s \cos(s) \geq 0$ on $s \in [0,2]$. 
    
    We conclude using Jensen's inequality:
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\cos(x+y) + \cos(x-y)}{2} = & \frac{f((x+y)^2)+f((x-y)^2)}{2} \\
        & \geq f\left( \frac{(x+y)^2+(x-y)^2}{2} \right) = \cos(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}).
    \end{align*}
    Equality can only happen for $(x + y)^2 = (x - y)^2$, i.e. $xy=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Half-angle reduction to $\cos x\cos y\ge\cos\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, then convexity of $\cos\sqrt t$ on $[0,4]$ and Jensen's inequality.

nodes.name: Bound on product of two axis rotations
nodes.statement:
For any $\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{R}$ one has 
\[
    \|R_x(\alpha)R_y(\beta)-\mathrm{Id}\| \leq  \sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}
\]
with equality only for $\alpha = \beta = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\|R_x(\alpha)R_y(\beta)-\mathrm{Id}\|\le\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}$.
nodes.label: lem:RxRy

nodes.name: Proof of the rotation product bound
nodes.statement_short: Write $R_xR_y$ as a conjugate rotation by $\Psi$, compare traces, and bound $|\Psi|$ with the Jensen-type lemma.

nodes.name: sqrt(2) perturbation bound for M and X
nodes.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $|\theta-\overline{\theta}|,|\varphi-\overline{\varphi}| \leq \varepsilon$ then 
$\|M(\theta, \varphi)-M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\|, \|X({\theta, \varphi})-X(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| < \sqrt{2}\varepsilon.$
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon$-perturbing $(\theta,\varphi)$ changes $M$ and $X$ by less than $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ in norm.
nodes.label: lem:sqrt2

nodes.name: Proof of the sqrt(2) bound
nodes.statement:
For $(\theta, \varphi) = (\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$ the result is trivial since $\varepsilon>0$. In the other case,
    recall the identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR2})
    \[
    M(\theta, \varphi) =
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix}
        \cdot R_y(\varphi) \cdot R_z(-\theta),
    \]
    and denote by $Z$ the $2 \times 3$ matrix on the rind-hand side.
    It follows that
    \begin{align*}
    \|M(\theta, \varphi)-M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| \leq \|Z\|\cdot \|R_y(\varphi) \cdot R_z(-\theta)- R_y(\overline{\varphi}) \cdot R_z(-\overline{\theta})\|
    \end{align*}
    from the sub-multiplicativity of the norm. Using $\|Z\|=1$ and that $R_y(-\varphi), R_z(\theta)$ are orthogonal we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \|M(\theta, \varphi)-M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| \leq \|\text{Id}-R_y(\overline{\varphi}-\varphi)R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|. 
\end{align*}
The right-hand side is strictly smaller than $\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2 + (\varphi-\overline{\varphi})^2} \leq \sqrt{2}\varepsilon$ by \cref{lem:RxRy} using that $(\theta, \varphi) \neq (\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$. 

    The proof for $\|X({\theta, \varphi})-X(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\|$ is analogous using the corresponding identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR1})    for $X({\theta, \varphi})$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $M$ through axis rotations (XMRfromR2), use orthogonality and the rotation product bound.

nodes.name: Positivity of scalar product under perturbation
nodes.statement:
Let $P \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P\| \leq 1$. Further, let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}, \theta, \varphi \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\overline{\theta}-\theta|, |\overline{\varphi} - \varphi| \leq \varepsilon$. If  
    \(
        \langle X(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}),P \rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon
    \)
    then
    \(
        \langle X(\theta, \varphi),P \rangle>0.
    \)
nodes.label: lem:XP>0

nodes.name: Proof of positivity under perturbation
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz together with the $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ bound.

nodes.name: Projection norm lower bound under perturbation
nodes.statement:
Let $P \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P\| \leq 1$. Further, let $\varepsilon, r>0$ and $\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}, \theta, \varphi \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\overline{\theta}-\theta|, |\overline{\varphi} - \varphi| \leq \varepsilon$. If  
    \(
        \| M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}) P \| > r + \sqrt{2}\varepsilon
    \)
    then
    \(
        \| M(\theta,\varphi) P \| > r.
    \)
nodes.label: lem:MP>r

nodes.name: Proof of projection norm lower bound
nodes.statement:
It follows from the triangle inequality that 
    \[
        \| M(\theta, \varphi) P \| \geq \| M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) P \| - \| M(\theta, \varphi) - M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})\| \|P\|,
    \]
    then the right-hand side is larger than $r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon - \sqrt{2}\varepsilon \cdot 1 = r$ by \cref{lem:sqrt2} and using that $\|P\| \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality together with the $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ bound.

nodes.name: sqrt(5) perturbation bound for RM
nodes.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $|\theta-\overline{\theta}|,|\varphi-\overline{\varphi}|,|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\leq\varepsilon$ then
    $\|R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)-R(\overline{\alpha})M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| < \sqrt{5} \varepsilon.$
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon$-perturbing $(\alpha,\theta,\varphi)$ changes $R(\alpha)M(\theta,\varphi)$ by less than $\sqrt5\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:sqrt5

nodes.name: Proof of the sqrt(5) bound
nodes.statement:
Recall the identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR3})
    \[
    R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)=
       \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix}
        R_z(\alpha) \cdot R_y(\varphi) \cdot R_z(-\theta)
    \] 
    to obtain like in the proof of \cref{lem:sqrt2}:
    \begin{align*}
        \|R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)-R(\overline{\alpha})M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| \leq \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi) - R_y(\overline{\varphi}) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|
    \end{align*}
    using the sub-multiplicativity of the norm.

    Now define   
    \[
        \Phi = \frac{\varphi\cdot |\theta-\overline{\theta}| +\overline{\varphi}\cdot |\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|}{|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|+|\theta-\overline{\theta}|},
    \]
    and obtain further using the triangle inequality and \cref{lem:RxRy}:
    \begin{align*}
        \|R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)-R(\overline{\alpha})M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| 
        &\leq \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi) - R_y(\Phi)\|+ \|R_y(\Phi)-R_y(\overline{\varphi}) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|\\
        &= \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi-\Phi) - \text{Id}\|+ \|\text{Id}-R_y(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|\\
        &\leq \sqrt{(\alpha-\overline{\alpha})^2+(\varphi-\Phi)^2}+\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2+(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi)^2}.
    \end{align*}
    Note that also by \cref{lem:RxRy} this inequality is strict except if both sides vanish.
    The definition of $\Phi$ conveniently implies after a small computation that 
    \[
        \sqrt{(\alpha-\overline{\alpha})^2+(\varphi-\Phi)^2}+\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2+(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi)^2} = \sqrt{\left(|\alpha - \overline{\alpha}|+|\theta - \overline{\theta}|\right)^2 + |\varphi-\overline{\varphi}|^2} \leq \sqrt{5}\varepsilon,
    \]
    which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Factor through axis rotations, split via an interpolating angle $\Phi$, and apply the rotation product bound twice.

nodes.name: Vertex-outside criterion for excluding a solution
nodes.statement:
Simply rephrasing this observation, we can say that if there exists a vertex $S \in \mathbf{P}$ and a vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that 
\[
    \langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S ,w\rangle > \max_{P \in \mathbf{P}} \langle M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P ,w\rangle,
\]
then $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ cannot be a solution to Rupert's problem.
nodes.statement_short: If some rotated projected vertex has larger scalar product with $w$ than every point of the other projection, the parameters are no solution.
assumptions:
if there exists a vertex $S \in \mathbf{P}$ and a vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that 
\[
    \langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S ,w\rangle > \max_{P \in \mathbf{P}} \langle M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P ,w\rangle,
\]
conclusions: then $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ cannot be a solution to Rupert's problem

nodes.name: Crude global exclusion criterion
nodes.statement:
For instance, a direct application of \cref{lem:sqrt2} and \cref{lem:sqrt5} shows that if 
\[
    \langle R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)S,w \rangle > \max_{P \in \mathbf{P}} \langle M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)P,w \rangle + (\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{5}) \rho \varepsilon
\]
for some pointsymmetric convex $\mathbf{P}$ of radius $\rho$, some $S \in \mathbf{P}$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|w\|=1$, then there cannot be a solution $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] $.
nodes.statement_short: A margin of $(\sqrt2+\sqrt5)\rho\varepsilon$ in the vertex-outside criterion excludes the whole $\varepsilon$-cube.
assumptions: for some pointsymmetric convex $\mathbf{P}$ of radius $\rho$, some $S \in \mathbf{P}$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|w\|=1$
conclusions: then there cannot be a solution $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] $

nodes.name: Global Theorem
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a pointsymmetric convex polyhedron with radius $\rho =1$ and let $S \in \mathbf{P}$. Further let $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $w\in\mathbb{R}^2$ be a unit vector. Denote $\overline{M_1} \coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $ \overline{M_2} \coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1}^{\theta} \coloneqq M^\theta(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $\overline{M_1}^{\varphi} \coloneqq M^\varphi(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$ and analogously for $\overline{M_2}^{\theta}, \overline{M_2}^{\varphi}$. Finally set
    \begin{align*}
        G& \coloneqq \langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} S,w \rangle - \varepsilon\cdot\big(|\langle R'(\overline{\alpha})  \overline{M_1} S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\theta S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\varphi S,w \rangle|\big)- 9\varepsilon^2/2,\\
        H_P & \coloneqq \langle \overline{M_2} P,w \rangle + \varepsilon\cdot\big(|\langle \overline{M_2}^\theta P,w \rangle|+|\langle  \overline{M_2}^\varphi P,w \rangle|\big) + 2\varepsilon^2, \quad \text{ for } P \in \mathbf{P}.
    \end{align*}
    If $G>\max_{P\in \mathbf{P}} H_P$ then there does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition (\ref{eq:rupert_condition}) with 
    $$(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in U \coloneqq [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5.$$
nodes.statement_short: If a vertex's projected scalar product with $w$ exceeds all of the other projection's, with first- and second-order error margins, no solution exists in the $\varepsilon$-cube.
assumptions: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a pointsymmetric convex polyhedron with radius $\rho =1$ and let $S \in \mathbf{P}$
conclusions:
then there does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition (\ref{eq:rupert_condition}) with 
    $$(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in U \coloneqq [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5.$$
nodes.label: thm:global

nodes.name: Global theorem for the octahedron
nodes.statement:
Consider the Octahedron $\mathbf{O} = \{ (\pm 1, 0,0), (0, \pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1) \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ and two projection directions $(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) = (0,0)$ and $(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) = (\pi/4,\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}))$. 
    We wish to apply \cref{thm:global} to show that with $\overline{\alpha}=0$ this choice of parameters does not yield a solution to Rupert's problem for $\mathbf{O}$ and, moreover, that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that there is also no solution $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha)$ with $|\overline{\theta}_i - \theta_i|,|\overline{\varphi}_i - \varphi_i|, |\alpha| \leq \varepsilon$ either. 
    In other words, the red projection in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron_glob} is not inside the black one, even after perturbing the projection parameters by some small $\varepsilon>0$.
    
    \begin{figure}[htb]
        \centering
        \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{pics/octa_global_label.pdf}
        \caption{Two projections of the Octahedron: one in direction $(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) = (0,0)$ (in red) and one in direction $(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) = (\pi/4, \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$ (in black).} \end{figure}
    
    Following \cref{thm:global} we first compute:
    \[
     \overline{M_1} =  \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 1 & 0 \\
    -1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}  \quad \text{ and } \quad \overline{M_2} = \begin{pmatrix}
    -\sqrt{2}/2 & \sqrt{2}/2 & 0 \\
    -\sqrt{6}/6 & -\sqrt{6}/6 & \sqrt{6}/3
\end{pmatrix}.
    \]
    Moreover, for the derivatives we find
    \[
        \overline{M_1}^\theta =  
\begin{pmatrix}
    -1 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & -1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \overline{M_1}^\varphi = 
\begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{ as well as}
    \]
    \[
        \overline{M_2}^\theta =  
\begin{pmatrix}
    -\sqrt{2}/2 & -\sqrt{2}/2 & 0 \\
    \sqrt{6}/6 & -\sqrt{6}/6 & 0
\end{pmatrix}  \quad \text{ and } \quad \overline{M_2}^\varphi = 
\begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 0 & 0 \\
    \sqrt{3}/3 & \sqrt{3}/3 & \sqrt{3}/3
\end{pmatrix}.
    \]
    Further note that $R(0) = \mathrm{Id}$ and $R'(0) = R(\pi/2)$. We choose $S = O_3 = (0,1,0)$ the preimage of the vertex on the very right in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron_glob} and $w = (1,0)$ the direction of $M(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1) S$.
    
    After a straightforward calculation we obtain 
    \[
        G = 1 - 9\varepsilon^2/2
    \]
    and
    \[
        H_P = 
        \begin{cases}
            2 \varepsilon ^2 \quad & \text{ for } P = M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) O_i \; \text{ with } \; i=1,6, \\
            \sqrt{2}/2 + \varepsilon \sqrt{2}/2 + 2 \varepsilon^2 \quad & \text{ for } P = M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) O_i \; \text{ with } \; i=3,4,\\
            -\sqrt{2}/2 + \varepsilon \sqrt{2}/2 + 2 \varepsilon^2 \quad & \text{ for } P = M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) O_i \; \text{ with } \; i=2,5.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    It is then obvious that $\max H_P$ is $\sqrt{2}/2 + \varepsilon \sqrt{2}/2 + 2 \varepsilon^2$ and that $G = 1 - 9\varepsilon^2/2 > \max H_P$ for small $\varepsilon$. Specifically, if $\varepsilon < 0.164$ then \cref{thm:global} can be applied and a solution in the region described above can be ruled out.

    We note that the strategy of the proof below --  applied to the current example -- is to show that the most right point in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron_glob} cannot move inside the black projection if the parameters $\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}$ are changed by at most $\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Applies the global theorem to two octahedron projections, showing no solution near them for $\varepsilon<0.164$.

nodes.name: Scalar product bound for points of a convex polygon
nodes.statement:
If $\mathcal{P} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is a convex polygon, $S \in \mathcal{P}^\circ$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ then
    \[
        \langle S ,w \rangle \leq \max_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \langle P ,w\rangle.
    \]
nodes.label: lem:hullscalarprod

nodes.name: Proof of the scalar product bound
nodes.statement:
Write $S = \sum_i \lambda_i P_i$ for $P_i \in \mathcal{P}$ the vertices of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\lambda_i \in [0,1)$ such that $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$. Moreover, denote $M \coloneqq \max_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \langle P ,w\rangle $. Then:
    \[
        \langle S ,w \rangle = \sum_i \lambda_i \langle P_i, w \rangle \leq M \cdot \sum_i \lambda_i = M. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $S$ as a convex combination of vertices and use linearity.

nodes.name: Partial derivatives of M
nodes.statement_short: $M^\theta$, $M^\varphi$ are the entrywise derivatives of $M(\theta,\varphi)$ in $\theta$ and $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Derivatives of rotation matrices
nodes.statement:
Moreover, in the same way we also write for the derivative of the rotation matrix in two dimensions:
\[
R'(\alpha) \coloneqq \frac{\mathrm{d}{}}{\mathrm{d}{}\alpha} R(\alpha) = 
    \begin{pmatrix} 
    -\sin(\alpha) & -\cos(\alpha) \\ 
    \cos(\alpha)& -\sin(\alpha)\\ 
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
and for the derivatives of the three-dimensional rotations along axes we analogously use:
\begin{align*}
R_{x}'(\alpha)\coloneqq 
    \begin{pmatrix} 
    0 & 0 & 0\\ 
    0 & -\sin(\alpha) & -\cos(\alpha)\\
    0 & \cos(\alpha) & -\sin(\alpha)
    \end{pmatrix}, & \qquad R_{y}'(\alpha)\coloneqq 
    \begin{pmatrix} 
    -\sin(\alpha) & 0 & -\cos(\alpha)\\
    0 & 0 & 0\\ 
    \cos(\alpha) & 0 & -\sin(\alpha) 
    \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \\
    R_{z}'(\alpha)\coloneqq &
    \begin{pmatrix} 
    -\sin(\alpha) & -\cos(\alpha) & 0 \\
    \cos(\alpha) & -\sin(\alpha) & 0\\
    0 & 0 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives of the 2D rotation $R$ and of the axis rotations $R_x,R_y,R_z$.

nodes.name: Second derivatives notation
nodes.statement: Similarly we shall denote the second derivatives by $M^{\theta \theta}(\theta, \varphi), M^{\theta \varphi}(\theta, \varphi), R''(\alpha), R_{x}''(\alpha)$, etc.

nodes.name: Derivatives of rotations have unit norm
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that all derivatives of the rotation matrices have unit norm, e.g., $\|R_{z}''(\alpha)\|= 1$.
conclusions: all derivatives of the rotation matrices have unit norm

nodes.name: Chain-rule identities for the derivatives of M
nodes.statement_short: $M^\theta$ and $M^\varphi$ factor through derivatives of axis rotations.

nodes.name: Second derivatives of the scalar product are bounded by 1
nodes.statement:
Let $S \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ be unit vectors and set $f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \langle R(x_3) M(x_1,x_2)S,w \rangle$. Then for all $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ and any $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ it holds that
    \[
        \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d} x_i \mathrm{d} x_j}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq 1.
    \]
nodes.label: lem:leq1

nodes.name: Proof of the second-derivative bound
nodes.statement:
We shall prove the statement for $(i,j)=(1,2)$ only as the other cases are analogous. First we rewrite $f(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ as
\[
    f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \left\langle 
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix} R_z(x_3) \cdot R_y(x_2) \cdot R_z(-x_1)S,w \right\rangle,
\]
then it follows from the chain rule that 
    \[
        \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d} x_1 \mathrm{d} x_2}(x_1,x_2,x_3) = -\left\langle 
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix} R_z(x_3) \cdot R_y'(x_2) \cdot R_z'(-x_1)S,w \right\rangle,
    \]
then the statement follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the bounds on the matrix norms and $\|S\| = \|w\| = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $f$ through axis rotations, differentiate with the chain rule, and apply Cauchy-Schwarz with unit-norm derivatives.

nodes.name: Partial derivative notation
nodes.statement: In the proof we will also use the following fact in which we write $\partial_{x_i}f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for the derivative of some differentiable $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with respect to $x_i$:

nodes.name: Second-order Taylor bound
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^2$-function and $x_1,\dots,x_n,y_1,\dots,y_n \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|x_1-y_1|,\dots,|x_n-y_n|\leq \varepsilon$. 
    If 
    \(
        \left|\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j}f(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| \leq 1
    \)
    for all $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ then
    \[
    |f(x_1,\dots,x_n)-f(y_1,\dots,y_n)|\leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^n |\partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)| + \frac{n^2}{2}\varepsilon^2.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: With Hessian entries bounded by 1, $|f(x)-f(y)|\le\varepsilon\sum|\partial_i f(x)|+n^2\varepsilon^2/2$.
nodes.label: lem:n2

nodes.name: Optimality of the constant n^2/2
nodes.statement: Note that the factor $n^2/2$ in this lemma is optimal as for the function $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=(x_1+\cdots + x_n)^2/2$ at $x_1=\cdots=x_n=0$ and $y_1=\cdots=y_n=\varepsilon$ equality holds.

nodes.name: Proof of the second-order Taylor bound
nodes.statement:
Let $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $y = (y_1,\dots,y_n)$. We define $g:[0,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ by
    \[
        g(t) = f\big(x_1(1-t)+y_1t, \dots ,x_n(1-t)+y_nt\big) = f(x(1-t)+yt)
    \]
    and observe that 
    \[
        g(1)-g(0)=\int_0^1g'(t)\text{d}t=\int_0^1\int_0^t g''(s)\text{d}s+g'(0)\text{d}t=g'(0)+\int_0^1\int_0^t g''(s)\text{d}s\text{d}t.
    \]
    Note that $|g(1)-g(0)|$ is exactly the term which needs to be bounded.
    The chain rule implies that 
    \[
        g'(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-x_i) \partial_{x_i} f(x(1-t)+yt),
    \]
    thus at $t=0$ we find
    \begin{align*}
    |g'(0)| \leq\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i-x_i| \cdot | \partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)| \leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^n |\partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)|. 
    \end{align*}
    For the second derivative of $g(t)$ we also get with the chain rule
    $$g''(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n(y_i-x_i)(y_j-x_j) \cdot \partial_{x_i} \partial_{x_j} f\big(x(1-t)+y t\big),$$
   which implies that
    $|g''(t)|\leq n^2 \varepsilon^2$.
    Altogether, one obtains
    \begin{align*}
      |f(x_1,\dots,x_n)-f(y_1,\dots,y_n)| & = |g(1)-g(0)| \leq |g'(0)|+\int_0^1\int_0^t |g''(s)|\text{d}s\text{d}t\\
      &\leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^n | \partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)| + \frac{n^2}{2}\varepsilon^2. \qquad \qedhere
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Restrict $f$ to the segment from $x$ to $y$, write $g(1)-g(0)$ via $g'(0)$ and a double integral of $g''$, and bound both.

nodes.name: Proof of the Global Theorem
nodes.statement:
We prove the statement by contradiction: Assume that there exists $S \in \mathbf{P}$ with a unit vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ like in the assumption and $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in U$ such that Rupert's condition is satisfied. As noted before, Rupert's condition and \cref{lem:hullscalarprod} imply in particular that 
    \[
        \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)P,w \rangle < \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle.
    \]
    We shall, however, show that the following sequence of inequalities yields the desired contradiction: 
    \[
        \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)P,w \rangle \stackrel{\text{(i)}}{\geq} \langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S,w \rangle\stackrel{\text{(ii)}}{\geq} G \stackrel{\text{(iii)}}{>}H\stackrel{\text{(iv)}}{\geq}\max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle.
    \]

    
    The inequality (i) is obvious and (iii) is an assumption of the theorem. To show inequality (ii) define the function 
    \[
        f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S/\|S\|,w \rangle = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S,w \rangle/\|S\|.
    \]
    Then \cref{lem:leq1} guarantees that 
    \[
        \left|\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq 1,
    \]
    for all $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ and any $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$; therefore \cref{lem:n2} applies and implies that
    \[
        |f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})-f(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\alpha)|\leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^3 |\partial_{x_i} f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})| + \frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^2,
    \]
    as $|\overline{\theta}_1-\theta_1|,|\overline{\varphi}_1-\varphi_1|,|\overline{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq \varepsilon$ by assumption. Multiplying the inequality with $\|S\|$ we get
    \begin{align*}
        |\langle R(a)  M({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle-\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S,w \rangle| & \\
       & \hspace{-6.5cm} \leq \varepsilon\cdot\bigg(|\langle R(\alpha)  M({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha})  M^\theta({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha})  M^\varphi({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|\bigg) +\frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^2\|S\|.
    \end{align*}
    From this and $\|S\|\leq 1$ the inequality (ii) follows.
    Finally, inequality (iv) can be shown in a similar way: for every $P \in \mathbf{P}$, again using \cref{lem:n2}, it holds that
    \[ 
        \langle   M({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle + \varepsilon\cdot\bigg(|\langle M^\theta({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle|+|\langle  M^\varphi({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle|\bigg)+ 2\varepsilon^2 \geq \langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: chain of inequalities (i)-(iv); (ii) and (iv) follow from the second-order Taylor bound with Hessian entries at most 1.

nodes.name: Projection direction notation
nodes.statement: Given $\theta, \varphi$, we shall write $X = X(\theta, \varphi)$ for the direction of a projection matrix $M = M(\theta, \varphi)$.

nodes.name: Pythagoras for projections
nodes.statement:
For any $P \in \mathbb{R}^3$ one has
    $\big\|M(\theta, \varphi) P\big\|^2=\|P\|^2-\langle X({\theta,\varphi}),P\rangle^2$.
nodes.label: lem:pythagoras

nodes.name: Proof of Pythagoras for projections
nodes.statement:
Define the matrix 
    \[
        A({\theta,\varphi}) \coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}
        M(\theta, \varphi)\\
        X({\theta,\varphi})^t
        \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}.
    \]
    Note that $A({\theta,\varphi}) \cdot A({\theta,\varphi})^t = \mathrm{Id}$, thus the matrix is orthogonal and hence it is length-preserving. We therefore obtain
    \[
        \|P\|^2=\|A({\theta,\varphi})P\|^2=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}
        M(\theta, \varphi)P\\
        \langle X({\theta, \varphi}),P\rangle
        \end{pmatrix}\right\|^2=\big\|M(\theta, \varphi) P\big\|^2+\langle X({\theta, \varphi}),P\rangle^2. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Stack $M$ and $X^t$ into an orthogonal $3\times3$ matrix, which preserves length.

nodes.name: Positive span (simplicial cone)
nodes.statement:
Given $v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{R}^n$ write $\mathrm{span}^+(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ for the set (simplicial cone) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ defined by 
    \[
        \mathrm{span}^+(v_1,\dots,v_n) = \Big\{ w \in \mathbb{R}^n \colon \exists \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n > 0 \text{ s.t. } w = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i v_i \Big\},
    \]
    which is the natural restriction of $\mathrm{span}(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ to positive weights.

nodes.name: Three scalar products cannot all increase
nodes.statement_short: For equal-norm $Y,Z$ in the positive cone of $V_1,V_2,V_3$, not all $\langle V_i,Y\rangle>\langle V_i,Z\rangle$.
nodes.label: lem:langles

nodes.name: Proof of the scalar products lemma
nodes.statement:
Let $V = (V_1|V_2|V_3) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ and assume by contradiction that all inequalities hold. This translates into
\begin{align} V^T Y \gg V^T Z,
\end{align}
where we use $x \gg y$ for vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^3$ if $x_1>y_1,x_2>y_2$ and $x_3>y_3.$ Moreover, let $\lambda, \nu \in \mathbb{R}^3_{>0}$ such that $Y = \lambda_1 V_1+\lambda_2V_2+\lambda_3V_3$ and
$Z = \nu_1 V_1+\nu_2V_2+\nu_3V_3$. In other words, we have 
\[
Y =  V \lambda  \quad \text{ and }  \quad Z =  V\nu .
\]
The assumption that $\|Y\| = \|Z\|$ translates therefore into
\[
\lambda^T V^T V \lambda = \nu^T V^T V \nu,
\]
and the inequalities $(\ref{ineq})$ rewrite as
\[
V^T V \lambda \gg V^T V \nu.
\]
Using this and the positivity of $\lambda,\nu \in \mathbb{R}^3$, we find a contradiction in 
\[
    \lambda^T V^T V \lambda > \lambda^T V^T V \nu = (\nu^T V^T V \lambda)^T > (\nu^TV^TV\nu)^T = \lambda^T V^T V \lambda.  \qedhere
\]
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: writing $Y=V\lambda$, $Z=V\nu$ with positive weights gives $\lambda^TV^TV\lambda>\lambda^TV^TV\lambda$.

nodes.name: Componentwise inequality V^T Y >> V^T Z
nodes.statement: V^T Y \gg V^T Z,
nodes.label: ineq

nodes.name: Bound on differences of scalar products
nodes.statement:
For $A,\overline{A},B,\overline{B}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $P_1,P_2\in \mathbb{R}^n$ it holds that
    \[
        |\langle AP_1,BP_2\rangle-\langle \overline{A}P_1,\overline{B}P_2\rangle|\leq \|P_1\|\cdot \|P_2\|\cdot \Big( \|A-\overline{A}\|\cdot \|\overline{B}\| +  \|\overline{A}\|\cdot \|B-\overline{B}\|+\|A-\overline{A}\|\cdot \|B-\overline{B}\|\Big).
    \]
nodes.label: lem:scalarprodbars

nodes.name: Proof of scalar product difference bound
nodes.statement_short: Expand bilinearly, then apply the triangle and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities and sub-multiplicativity.

nodes.name: Symmetric bound on differences of scalar products
nodes.statement:
For $A,B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $P_1,P_2\in \mathbb{R}^n$ one has
    $$|\langle AP_1,AP_2\rangle-\langle BP_1,BP_2\rangle|\leq \|P_1\|\cdot \|P_2\|\cdot \|A-B\|\cdot \bigg(\|A\|+\|B\| + \|A-B\|\bigg).$$
nodes.label: lem:absscalar

nodes.name: Proof of the symmetric bound
nodes.statement_short: Apply the previous bound in both orders of $A,B$ and average.

nodes.name: Origin in triangle via positive combination
nodes.statement:
Note that for a non-degenerate triangle this is equivalent to the existence of $a,b,c > 0$ such that
\[
    aA+bB+cC=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\0
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
conclusions:
this is equivalent to the existence of $a,b,c > 0$ such that
\[
    aA+bB+cC=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\0
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]

nodes.name: Origin-in-triangle criterion
nodes.statement:
Let $A,B,C\in \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that $
    \langle R({\pi/2}) A,B\rangle,
    \langle R({\pi/2}) B,C\rangle,
    \langle R({\pi/2}) C,A\rangle >0$. Then the origin lies strictly in the triangle $ABC$.
nodes.statement_short: If the three cyclic cross products $\langle R(\pi/2)A,B\rangle$ etc. are positive, the origin is strictly inside triangle $ABC$.
assumptions:
Let $A,B,C\in \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that $
    \langle R({\pi/2}) A,B\rangle,
    \langle R({\pi/2}) B,C\rangle,
    \langle R({\pi/2}) C,A\rangle >0$
conclusions: Then the origin lies strictly in the triangle $ABC$
nodes.label: lem:origintriangle

nodes.name: Proof of the origin-in-triangle criterion
nodes.statement:
Write $A=(A_1,A_2)^t$, $B=(B_1,B_2)^t$, $C=(C_1,C_2)^t$ and consider the two vectors $v_1=(A_1,B_1,C_1)^t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $v_2=(A_2,B_2,C_2)^t \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Now set $(a,b,c)^t \coloneqq v_1\times v_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to be the cross product of $v_1$ and $v_2$. By the orthogonality property of the cross product we obtain
    \[
        aA+bB+cC=\big(A| B| C\big)\cdot (v_1\times v_2)=\begin{pmatrix}
            v_1^t\\ v_2^t
        \end{pmatrix} (v_1\times v_2)=\begin{pmatrix}
            0\\0
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \]
    Additionally observe that
    \[
        \begin{pmatrix}
            a\\b\\c
        \end{pmatrix}= v_1\times v_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
            A_1\\B_1\\C_1
        \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}
            A_2\\B_2\\C_2
        \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}
            B_1C_2-C_1B_2\\C_1A_2-A_1C_2\\A_1B_2-B_1A_2
        \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}
            \langle R(\pi/2) B,C\rangle\\
            \langle R(\pi/2) C,A\rangle\\
            \langle R(\pi/2) A,B\rangle
        \end{pmatrix},
    \]
    thus $a,b,c >0$.
nodes.statement_short: The cross product of the coordinate vectors gives weights $(a,b,c)$ with $aA+bB+cC=0$, equal to the three positive quantities.

nodes.name: epsilon-spanning points
nodes.statement_short: Three points are $\varepsilon$-spanning if the three cyclic cross products of their projections exceed $2\varepsilon(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)$.
nodes.label: def:eps-spanning

nodes.name: epsilon-spanning implies positive span of X
nodes.statement:
Let $P_1, P_2, P_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P_1\|,\|P_2\|,\|P_3\| \leq 1$ be $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$ and let $\theta, \varphi \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|\theta - \overline{\theta}|, |\varphi - \overline{\varphi}| \leq \varepsilon$. Assume that $\langle X(\theta, \varphi), P_i \rangle > 0$ for $i=1,2,3$. Then 
    \[
        X(\theta, \varphi) \in \mathrm{span}^+(P_1, P_2, P_3).
    \]
nodes.statement_short: For $\varepsilon$-spanning points in front of the perturbed direction, $X(\theta,\varphi)$ lies in their positive cone.
assumptions: Let $P_1, P_2, P_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P_1\|,\|P_2\|,\|P_3\| \leq 1$ be $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$
nodes.label: lem:eps-spanning

nodes.name: Proof that epsilon-spanning implies positive span
nodes.statement:
It follows from the definition of $\varepsilon$-spanning and \cref{lem:sqrt2} that 
    \begin{align} \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_1,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{2}\rangle > 0, \nonumber \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_2,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{3}\rangle > 0, \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_3,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{1}\rangle > 0, \nonumber
    \end{align}
    using \cref{lem:scalarprodbars} on $A=R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi), B =  M(\theta, \varphi)$ analogously for $\overline{A}, \overline{B}$ with the fact that $\|R(\pi/2)\|=1$ and $\|P_1\|,\|P_2\|,\|P_3\| \leq 1$. Thus, \cref{lem:origintriangle} implies that the origin $O$ is strictly inside the triangle $\Delta(M(\theta, \varphi) P_1, M(\theta, \varphi) P_2, M(\theta, \varphi) P_3)$.
    It follows that there exist $a,b,c >0$ such~that 
    \begin{align} aM(\theta,\varphi)P_1 + bM(\theta,\varphi)P_2 + cM(\theta,\varphi)P_3 = O.
    \end{align}
    Consider the point $S = aP_1 + bP_2 + cP_3\in \mathbb{R}^3$. From (\ref{eq:Ybarkernel}) it follows that $S \in \ker M(\theta,\varphi)$. However, since $X \coloneqq X(\theta, \varphi) \in \ker M(\theta,\varphi)$ as well, we get that $S = \lambda X(\theta, \varphi)$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. It follows that
    \[
        \lambda = \langle X, \lambda X \rangle = \langle X, S \rangle = a \langle X, P_1\rangle + b \langle X, P_2\rangle + c \langle X, P_3\rangle > 0,
    \]
    and, consequently, that $X(\theta, \varphi) = \frac{1}{\lambda}S \in \mathrm{span}^+(P_1, P_2, P_3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Perturbation bounds keep the origin inside the projected triangle; the positive combination lies in $\ker M$, so it is a positive multiple of $X$.

nodes.name: Perturbed spanning inequalities
nodes.statement:
\langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_1,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{2}\rangle > 0, \nonumber \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_2,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{3}\rangle > 0, \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_3,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{1}\rangle > 0, \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:originintraiangle

nodes.name: Projected positive combination vanishes
nodes.statement: aM(\theta,\varphi)P_1 + bM(\theta,\varphi)P_2 + cM(\theta,\varphi)P_3 = O.
nodes.label: eq:Ybarkernel

nodes.name: Open disc
nodes.statement: For $\delta > 0$ and $\overline{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ we define $\mathrm{Disc}_{\delta}(\overline{Q})$ to be the open disk with center $\overline{Q}$ and radius~$\delta$.

nodes.name: Perturbed projections stay in a disc
nodes.statement:
Let $P, Q \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P\|, \|Q\| \leq 1$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$, then set
    \[
        T \coloneqq \left(R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) P + M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) Q\right)/2 \in \mathbb{R}^2,
    \]
    and $\delta \geq \|T - M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) Q\|$. Finally, let $\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|\overline{\theta}_1-\theta_1|, |\overline{\varphi}_1 - \varphi_1|, |\overline{\theta}_2-\theta_2|, |\overline{\varphi}_2-\varphi_2|, |\overline{\alpha} - \alpha| \leq \varepsilon$. Then $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1, \varphi_1) P, M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q \in \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon}(T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under $\varepsilon$-perturbation, both projected points stay within $\delta+\sqrt5\varepsilon$ of their midpoint $T$.
nodes.label: lem:inCirc

nodes.name: Proof of the disc lemma
nodes.statement:
By the triangle inequality and \cref{lem:sqrt5} we have
    \begin{align*}
        \| R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1) P - T \| & \leq \| R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1) P - R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) P \| + \| R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) P - T \|\\
        & \leq \| R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1) - R(\overline{\alpha}) M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) \| \cdot \|P\| + \delta < \sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta.
    \end{align*}
    Similarly, using \cref{lem:sqrt2} we also find that 
    \[
        \| M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q - T \| < \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + \delta < \sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality with the $\sqrt5\varepsilon$ and $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ bounds.

nodes.name: delta-locally maximally distant vertex
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a convex polygon and $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ one of its vertices. Assume that for some $\overline{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ it holds that $Q \in \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta}(\overline{Q})$, i.e. $\|Q - \overline{Q}\| < \delta$. Define $\mathrm{Sect}_\delta(\overline{Q}) \coloneqq \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta}(\overline{Q}) \cap \mathcal{P}^\circ$ as the intersection between $\mathrm{Disc}_{\delta}(\overline{Q})$ and the interior of the convex hull of $\mathcal{P}$.
    
    Moreover, $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ is called \emph{$\delta$-locally maximally distant with respect to $\overline{Q}$ ($\delta$-LMD$(\overline{Q})$)} if for all $A \in \mathrm{Sect}_\delta(\overline{Q})$ it holds that $\|Q\| > \|A\|$.
nodes.statement_short: A vertex $Q$ is $\delta$-LMD w.r.t. $\overline Q$ if it is farther from the origin than every interior point of the polygon in the $\delta$-disc.
nodes.label: def:LMD

nodes.name: Acute-angle criterion for LMD
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a convex polygon and $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ be one of its vertices. Let $\overline{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|Q - \overline{Q}\| < \delta$ for some $\delta>0$. Assume that for some $r > 0 $ such that $\|Q\| > r$ it holds that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle Q, Q - P_j \rangle}{\|Q\|\|Q - P_j\|} \geq \delta/r,
    \]
    for all other vertices $P_j \in \mathcal{P} \setminus Q$. Then $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ is $\delta$-locally maximally distant with respect to $\overline{Q}$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\cos\angle(O,Q,P_j)\ge\delta/r$ for all other vertices and $\|Q\|>r$, then $Q$ is $\delta$-LMD.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a convex polygon and $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ be one of its vertices

for some $r > 0 $ such that $\|Q\| > r$ it holds that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle Q, Q - P_j \rangle}{\|Q\|\|Q - P_j\|} \geq \delta/r,
    \]
    for all other vertices $P_j \in \mathcal{P} \setminus Q$
conclusions: Then $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ is $\delta$-locally maximally distant with respect to $\overline{Q}$
nodes.label: lem:LMD

nodes.name: Proof of the LMD criterion
nodes.statement:
Let $A \in \mathrm{Sect}_\delta(\overline{Q}) = \mathrm{Disc}_\delta(\overline{Q}) \cap \mathcal{P}^\circ$. We need to show that $\|A\| < \|Q\|$. By the cosine theorem in the triangle $\Delta OQA$ it holds that 
    \[
        \| A \|^2 = \|Q\|^2 + \|Q - A\|^2 - 2\|Q\|\|Q - A\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)).
    \]
    Or, equivalently, that 
    \[
        \|A\|^2 - \|Q\|^2 = \|Q - A\| \cdot (\|Q - A\| - 2\|Q\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A))).
    \]
    Now observe that $\angle(O,Q,A) < \angle(O,Q,P_j)$ for some vertex $P_j \in \mathcal{P} \setminus Q$ because $A \in \mathcal{P}^\circ$. Moreover, recall that 
    \[
    \cos(\angle(O,Q,P_j)) = \frac{\langle Q, Q - P_j \rangle}{\|Q\|\|Q - P_j\|} \geq \delta/r,
    \]
    thus $\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)) \geq \delta/r$. We also have that $\|Q\| \geq r$ by assumption and $\|Q - A\| < 2\delta$ because both $Q, A \in \mathrm{Disc}_\delta(\overline{Q})$. We conclude that 
    \[
        \|Q - A\| - 2\|Q\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)) < 2\delta - 2r\cdot\delta/r = 0,
    \]
    therefore $\|A\|^2 - \|Q\|^2 < 0$ and $\|A\| < \|Q\|$
nodes.statement_short: Cosine theorem in triangle $OQA$ with the angle bound shows $\|A\|^2-\|Q\|^2<0$.

nodes.name: Cosine perturbation bound
nodes.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\theta,\overline{\theta}, \varphi, \overline{\varphi} \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|\theta - \overline{\theta}|, |\varphi - \overline{\varphi}| \leq \varepsilon$. Define $M = M(\theta, \varphi)$ and $\overline{M} = M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$ and let $P, Q \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|P\|, \|Q\| \leq 1$. Assume\footnote{In a first version of this manuscript we were lacking this assumption and we thank \href{https://dwrensha.ws/}{David Renshaw} for pointing~it~out.} that 
    \[
    \frac{\langle \overline{M} P,\overline{M} (P-Q)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|P-Q\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M} P\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M}(P-Q)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)} > 0, 
    \]
    then:
    \[
        \frac{\langle {M} P,{M} (P-Q)\rangle}{\|{M} P\| \cdot \|{M}(P-Q)\|} \geq 
        \frac{\langle \overline{M} P,\overline{M} (P-Q)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|P-Q\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M} P\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M}(P-Q)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)}. 
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on the cosine of the angle at $MP$ for perturbed $(\theta,\varphi)$ in terms of quantities at the centre.
assumptions:
Assume\footnote{In a first version of this manuscript we were lacking this assumption and we thank \href{https://dwrensha.ws/}{David Renshaw} for pointing~it~out.} that 
    \[
    \frac{\langle \overline{M} P,\overline{M} (P-Q)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|P-Q\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M} P\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M}(P-Q)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)} > 0, 
    \]
nodes.label: lem:coss

nodes.name: Proof of the cosine perturbation bound
nodes.statement:
We will show that the numerator of the left-hand side is bigger than the one of the right-hand side, and that the factors in the denominator are smaller. We also show that the left-hand side is well-defined as $MP, M(P-Q) \neq 0$.

We apply \cref{lem:absscalar} to $A = M, B = \overline{M}$ and $P_1 = P, P_2 = P-Q$:
\begin{align*}
|\langle {M} P,{M} (P-Q) \rangle - \langle \overline{M} P,\overline{M} (P-Q)\rangle | & \leq \|P\| \cdot \|P - Q\| \cdot \| M - \overline{M} \| \cdot (\|M\| + \|\overline{M}\| + \| M - \overline{M} \|) \\
& \leq 1 \cdot \| P - Q \| \cdot \sqrt{2}\varepsilon \cdot (1 + 1 + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon),
\end{align*}
and observe the claim for the numerator using the triangle inequality. In particular, $\langle {M} P,{M} (P-Q)\rangle > 0$, thus $MP$ and $M(P-Q)$ are non-zero, and the denominator does not~vanish.

For the first factor in the denominator we simply have 
\[
\| \overline{M} P \| \geq \| M P \| - \| MP - \overline{M}P \| \geq \| M P \| - \| M - \overline{M} \| \cdot \|P\| \geq \|MP\| - \sqrt{2} \varepsilon,
\]
with the triangle inequality and \cref{lem:sqrt2}. For the other factor we obtain similarly 
\[
\| \overline{M} (P-Q) \| \geq \| M (P-Q) \| - \| M - \overline{M} \| \cdot \|P-Q\| \geq \|M(P-Q)\| - 2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon,
\]
using that $\|P-Q\| \leq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the numerator with the symmetric scalar-product bound and each denominator factor with the $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ bound.

nodes.name: Congruent triples
nodes.statement: Two triples of points $P_1, P_2, P_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are called \emph{congruent} if there exists an orthonormal matrix $L$ such that $P_i = LQ_i$ for $i=1,2,3$.

nodes.name: Gram-matrix criterion for congruence
nodes.statement:
Let $P_1,P_2,P_3, Q_1,Q_2,Q_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Define the $3 \times 3$ matrices $P \coloneqq (P_1|P_2|P_3)$ and $Q \coloneqq (Q_1|Q_2|Q_3)$ and assume that $Q$ is invertible. 
    Then $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent if and only if $P^t P = Q^t Q$.
conclusions: Then $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent if and only if $P^t P = Q^t Q$
equivalent_conditions: $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent
nodes.label: lem:congruent

nodes.name: Gram-matrix reformulation of congruence
nodes.statement: Note that $P^t P = Q^t Q$ is equivalent to saying that $\langle P_i,P_j\rangle = \langle Q_i,Q_j\rangle$ for all $1 \leq i,j \leq 3$. Moreover, the condition on invertibility of $Q$ can be dropped, however then the proof becomes somewhat less straightforward.

nodes.name: Proof of the congruence criterion
nodes.statement:
If $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent then $\langle P_i,P_j\rangle = \langle LQ_i,LQ_j\rangle = \langle Q_i,Q_j\rangle$, thus $P^t P = Q^t Q$.
    For the other direction, we claim that $L \coloneqq PQ^{-1}$ is orthonormal and satisfies that $P_i = LQ_i$ for all $i=1,2,3$.  
    Indeed,  $L^t L = (PQ^{-1})^t (PQ^{-1}) = (Q^t)^{-1} P^t P Q^{-1} = \mathrm{Id}$ and it holds that $LQ=PQ^{-1}Q=P$, thus $LQ_i = P_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Congruence preserves inner products; conversely $L=PQ^{-1}$ is orthonormal.

nodes.name: Local Theorem
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a polyhedron with radius $\rho=1$ and $P_1, P_2, P_3, Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 \in \mathbf{P}$ be not necessarily distinct. Assume that $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent.

    Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$, then set $\overline{X_1} \coloneqq X(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{X_2} \coloneqq X(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1} \coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{M_2} \coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$.
    Assume that there exist $\sigma_P, \sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$ such that 
    \[
        (-1)^{\sigma_P} \langle \overline{X_1},P_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon \quad \text{and} \quad
        (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2} , Q_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon, \tag{A$_\varepsilon$}
    \]
    for all $i=1,2,3$.
    Moreover, assume that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$.
    Finally, assume that for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $Q_j \in \mathbf{P} \setminus Q_i$ it holds~that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} Q_i,\overline{M_2} (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta}{r}, \tag{B$_\varepsilon$}
    \]
    for some $r >0$ such that $\min_{i=1,2,3}\| \overline{M_2} Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon$ and for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ with 
    \[
        \delta \geq \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} P_i - \overline{M_2} Q_i\right\|/2.
    \]
    Then there exists no solution to Rupert's problem $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset  M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)\mathbf{P}^\circ$ with 
    \[
        (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] \coloneqq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5.
    \]
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem
nodes.statement_short: Congruent $\varepsilon$-spanning triples in front of both projections with a locally-maximally-distant condition exclude all solutions in the $\varepsilon$-cube.
assumptions: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a polyhedron with radius $\rho=1$
Assume that $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent

Assume that there exist $\sigma_P, \sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$ such that 
    \[
        (-1)^{\sigma_P} \langle \overline{X_1},P_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon \quad \text{and} \quad
        (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2} , Q_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon, \tag{A$_\varepsilon$}
    \]
    for all $i=1,2,3$

assume that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$

Finally, assume that for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $Q_j \in \mathbf{P} \setminus Q_i$ it holds~that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} Q_i,\overline{M_2} (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta}{r}, \tag{B$_\varepsilon$}
    \]
    for some $r >0$ such that $\min_{i=1,2,3}\| \overline{M_2} Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon$ and for some $\delta \in \mathbb{R}$ with 
    \[
        \delta \geq \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} P_i - \overline{M_2} Q_i\right\|/2.
    \]
conclusions:
Then there exists no solution to Rupert's problem $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset  M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)\mathbf{P}^\circ$ with 
    \[
        (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\varepsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\varepsilon] \coloneqq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5.
    \]
nodes.label: thm:local

nodes.name: Local theorem for the octahedron
nodes.statement:
Consider the Octahedron $\mathbf{O} = \{ (\pm 1, 0,0), (0, \pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1) \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ and the projection direction $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) = (\pi/4,\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}))$. The polygon $M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) \mathbf{O}$ is depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron}. We enumerate the vertices $O_1,\dots,O_6$ of $\mathbf{O}$ in such a way that $O_1,O_2,O_3$ have nonnegative coordinates. The goal of this example is to use \cref{thm:local} to show that there exists an $\varepsilon>0$ such that there is no solution $\Psi$ to Rupert's problem for $\mathbf{O}$ with 
\[
\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha) \in U = [\overline{\varphi} \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\theta} \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\varphi} \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\theta} \pm \varepsilon, \pm \varepsilon].
\]

\begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{pics/octa_local_label.pdf}
    \caption{The projection of the octahedron $\mathbf{O}$ in direction $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) = (\pi/4,\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$.} \end{figure}

In order to apply \cref{thm:local} we choose $P_i=Q_i = O_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ as well as $\overline{\theta}_1 = \overline{\theta}_2 = \overline{\theta} = \pi/4$, $\overline{\varphi}_1 = \overline{\varphi}_2 = \overline{\varphi} = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$ and $\overline{\alpha}=0$. This means that
\[
\overline{M_1} = \overline{M_2} = \begin{pmatrix}
    -\sqrt{2}/2 & \sqrt{2}/2 & 0 \\
    -\sqrt{6}/6 & -\sqrt{6}/6 & \sqrt{6}/3
\end{pmatrix} \quad \text{ and } \quad \overline{X_1} = \overline{X_2} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{t}/\sqrt{3}.
\]
Since $\langle \overline{X_1}, O_i \rangle = 1/\sqrt{3}$ for $i=1,2,3$ it follows that $\sigma_P = \sigma_Q=0$ and $(A_\varepsilon)$ is fulfilled for epsilon small enough. In Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron} this simply means that the points $\overline{M_1} O_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ are ``in front'' of the projection. 

Next we need to check that $O_1,O_2,O_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$. Heuristically speaking, this simply means that the origin is inside the triangle $\Delta(\overline{M_1} O_1,\overline{M_1} O_2,\overline{M_1} O_3)$ even after exchanging $\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}$ with any possible $(\theta, \varphi) \in [\overline{\theta} \pm \varepsilon,\overline{\varphi} \pm \varepsilon]$. To verify this rigorously, we compute
\[
\langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} O_1, \overline{M_1} O_2\rangle = 1/\sqrt{3},
\]
and similarly for the other two conditions in \cref{def:eps-spanning}. Thus, the $\varepsilon$-spanning condition is satisfied as long as $1/\sqrt{3} > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon)$.

For the last condition (B$_\varepsilon$) if we fix without loss of generality $Q_i = O_1$ the left-hand side becomes:
\begin{align*}
  \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} O_1,\overline{M_2} (O_1-O_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|O_1-O_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} O_1\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(O_1-O_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)}  = 
  \begin{cases}
  \frac{1-2 \varepsilon  \sqrt{2}\, (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon )}{(\sqrt{6}/{3}+\varepsilon  \sqrt{2}) (\sqrt{2}+2 \varepsilon  \sqrt{2})} \quad \text{ for } j=2,3,\\
  \frac{{1}/{3}-2 \varepsilon  \sqrt{2}\, (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon )}{({\sqrt{6}}/{3}+\varepsilon  \sqrt{2}) \left({\sqrt{6}}/{3}+2 \varepsilon  \sqrt{2}\right)} \quad \text{ for } j=4,5,\\
  \frac{{4}/{3}-4 \varepsilon  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon )}{({\sqrt{6}}/{3}+\varepsilon  \sqrt{2}) ({2 \sqrt{6}}/{3}+2 \varepsilon  \sqrt{2})} \quad \text{ for } j=6.
  \end{cases}
\end{align*}
Note that for $\varepsilon$ small these expressions are approximately $\sqrt{3}/2, 1/2$ and $1$ respectively. For the right-hand side note that $\delta=0$ and if we choose $r < \|\overline{M_1} O_i\| = \sqrt{6}/3$ there will exist $\varepsilon>0$ which satisfies $\|\overline{M_1} O_i\| > r + \sqrt{2}\varepsilon$. Moreover, since $\sqrt{5}\varepsilon/r$ becomes arbitrarily small, (B$_\varepsilon$) holds for small enough $\varepsilon$. Following \cref{sec:lmds} this computation simply shows that $\overline{M_1} O_i$ are locally maximally distant points (also after exchanging $\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi}$ with any possible $\theta, \varphi \in [\overline{\theta} \pm \varepsilon, \overline{\varphi} \pm \varepsilon]$), because the angles $\angle (O,O_1,O_j)$ for $j=2,3,4,5,6$ in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron} are approximately $60^\circ, 30^\circ$, or $0^\circ$, in particular acute.

Altogether we have have proven that there is no ``local'' solution to Rupert's problem for the Octahedron from the direction $(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi}) = (\pi/4,\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$. We can also effectively choose, for example, $r=0.7$ and $\varepsilon=0.05$ to satisfy all appearing inequalities.

We also mention that if $(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1) = (\pi/4, \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}))$ but $(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2) = (\pi/4, \pi - \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}))$ then the two projections look still like in Figure~\ref{fig:octahedron}, however then we would need to take $P_i = O_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ but $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3) = (O_1, O_5, O_4)$ and verify that these points are congruent. Also, in this case, $\sigma_Q = 1$.

Finally, note that the proof of \cref{thm:local} crucially uses \cref{lem:langles} in combination with \cref{lem:pythagoras}, which in the context of this example simply state that the three distances $\|MO_1\|$, $\|MO_2\|$, $\|MO_3\|$ cannot all (locally) simultaneously increase. An even simpler way to see this exists, since $O_1, O_2, O_3$ are orthogonal to each other and of equal length -- in this case it holds that 
\[
    \|MO_1\|^2 + \|MO_2\|^2 + \|MO_3\|^2 = 2.
\]
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem
nodes.statement_short: Applies the local theorem to the octahedron viewed along $(1,1,1)$, e.g. with $r=0.7$, $\varepsilon=0.05$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Local Theorem
nodes.statement:
Assume by contradiction that there exists a $\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha) \in U$ which solves Rupert's problem. By assumption $(P_1,P_2,P_3)$ and $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)$ are congruent, thus there exists an orthonormal matrix $L \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ with $P_i  = LQ_i$ for all $i=1,2,3$. Set $Y \coloneqq X(\theta_1, \varphi_1)$ and $Z \coloneqq K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2)$, where $K \coloneqq (-1)^{\sigma_P + \sigma_Q}L$, so it is easy to see that $\|Y\|=\|Z\|=1$. Moreover, let $\overline{P_i} = (-1)^{\sigma_P} P_i$ and $\overline{Q_i} = (-1)^{\sigma_Q} Q_i$, so that $\overline{P_i} = K\overline{Q_i}$. 
    
    We shall show that 
        \begin{align} Y,Z \in \mathrm{span}^+(\overline{P_1},\overline{P_2},\overline{P_3})
        \end{align}
        and that
        \begin{align} \langle Y, \overline{P_i} \rangle > \langle Z, \overline{P_i} \rangle \text{ for each } i=1,2,3,
        \end{align}
        then \cref{lem:langles} yields the desired contradiction. \\    

    First observe that (A$_\varepsilon$) and \cref{lem:XP>0} imply that
    \begin{equation} \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle, \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle > 0.
    \end{equation}
    Now (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) for $Y = X(\theta_1, \varphi_1)$ follows from \cref{lem:eps-spanning}. By the same argument we also get that 
    \[
        X(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \in \mathrm{span}^+(\overline{Q_1},\overline{Q_2},\overline{Q_3}).
    \]
    However, then (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) also immediately follows for $Z = K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2)$ as $\overline{P_i} = K \overline{Q_i}$.\\

    We proceed with proving (\ref{eq:angles_fin}). First note that by assumption $\| \overline{M_2} Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon$, thus  \cref{lem:MP>r} shows that 
    \(
        \| M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \| > r.
    \)
    Define 
    \[
        T_i \coloneqq \left(R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} P_i + \overline{M_2} Q_i\right)/2 \in \mathbb{R}^2,
    \]
    for $i=1,2,3$ so that by assumption $\|T_i - \overline{M_2} Q_i\| \leq \delta$. Then also set
    \[
        \mathrm{Disc}_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon}(T_i) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^2: \| x - T_i \| < \delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon \}.
    \] 
    By \cref{lem:inCirc} it holds that $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1, \varphi_2) P_i, M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i$.
    Moreover, as the right-hand side in (B$_\varepsilon$) is positive, \cref{lem:coss} implies that 
    \[
    \frac{\langle M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i,M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle}{\|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i\| \cdot \|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)(Q_i-Q_j)\|} \geq 
    \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} Q_i,\overline{M_2} (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)},
    \]
    Thus, using assumption (B$_\varepsilon$), the left-hand side of this inequality is also larger than $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon)/r$. \cref{lem:LMD} now implies that $M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P}$ is $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon$)-LMD with respect to $T_i$. We obtain that for any $A \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ it holds that $\|A\| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$.

    Recall that by contradiction we assumed that $\Psi$ is a solution to Rupert's problem, thus, in particular, $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ and it follows that $A = R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$.
    We conclude that $ \| M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$. Now \cref{lem:pythagoras} implies that $ \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), P_i \rangle^2 > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), Q_i \rangle^2$ and (\ref{eq:YPiZPi>0_fin}) implies that 
    \[
        \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle.
    \]
    We conclude that (\ref{eq:angles_fin}) holds because
    \[
        \langle Y, \overline{P_i} \rangle = \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle>
        \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), K\overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle Z, \overline{P_i} \rangle. \qedhere
    \]

nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: both perturbed directions lie in the positive cone of the triple while all three scalar products strictly decrease, contradicting the scalar products lemma. LMD of the $Q_i$ gives the strict decrease via Pythagoras.

nodes.statement: \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle, \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle > 0.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem
