The Ruperthedron has the following two properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item [1)] $\mathbf{RUP}$ is Rupert and its Nieuwland number\footnote{For the definition of Nieuwland number we refer to \cite{StYu23}.} is at least $1.003$.
        \item [2)] There does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition of $\mathbf{RUP}$ with 
        $$|\theta_1-\theta_2|,|\varphi_1-\varphi_2|,|\alpha|\leq 0.0006 \eqqcolon \omega.$$
    \end{itemize}
    In particular, $\mathbf{RUP}$ is Rupert but not locally Rupert.
nodes.statement_short: RUP is Rupert with Nieuwland number at least 1.003, but has no solution with $|\theta_1-\theta_2|,|\varphi_1-\varphi_2|,|\alpha|\le0.0006$.
conclusions: $\mathbf{RUP}$ is Rupert and its Nieuwland number\footnote{For the definition of Nieuwland number we refer to \cite{StYu23}.} is at least $1.003$

There does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition of $\mathbf{RUP}$ with 
        $$|\theta_1-\theta_2|,|\varphi_1-\varphi_2|,|\alpha|\leq 0.0006 \eqqcolon \omega.$$
In particular, $\mathbf{RUP}$ is Rupert but not locally Rupert
nodes.label: thm:main2

nodes.name: Proof that the Ruperthedron is Rupert but not locally Rupert
nodes.statement:
A solution for $\mathbf{RUP}$ can be found using the methods described in \cite{StYu23}. Specifically, it can be checked using a computer algebra software that
    \[
        (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)=(0.29,0.29,0.02,2.27,-1.02)
    \]
    is a solution for $\mathbf{RUP}$'s Rupert's property and that it has Nieuwland number greater than $1.003$. This proves (1).

    Using the same symmetries described in \cref{lem:symmetries}, it is clear that we can assume $\theta_1\in[0,2\pi/15], \varphi_1\in[0,\pi/2]$ and $\alpha \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.
    We define the sequence of points $A_k \coloneqq \omega\cdot k \in \mathbb{R}$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Note, that $A_{699}>2\pi/15$ and $A_{2618}>\pi/2$. We further define the five-dimensional closed cubes $B_{i,j}\subset \mathbb{R}^5$ for $i=0,\dots,699$, $j=0,\dots, 2618$ by
    \[
        B_{i,j} \coloneqq [A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, 0\pm\omega].
    \]
    If a solution $\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)$ would exist as stated in (2) then, for some $0\leq i\leq 699$ and some $0\leq j\leq 2618$, it would hold that $\Psi \in B_{i,j}$. 
    
    However, similarly to the solution tree for \cref{thm:main}, we can construct regions $C_k\subset \mathbb{R}^5$ for $0\leq k \leq 3534$ such that each $B_{i,j}$ is a subset of at least one $C_k$, and such that it is possible to prove using the rational local \cref{thm:local_rational} that there does not exist a solution $\Psi \in C_k$ for all $k$. The definition of $(C_k)_{0 \leq k \leq 3534}$, the list which $B_{i,j}$  lies within which $C_k$ and the verification code are stored on \href{https://github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}{www.github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit an explicit solution; then cover all near-local parameters by cubes, each excluded with the rational local theorem by computer.

nodes.name: Dual of the Ruperthedron is locally Rupert
nodes.statement: We note that the Ruperthedron is a natural candidate for disproving Conjecture 2 in \cite{Scott2022}: We believe that its dual (for any reasonable definition of this term) is locally Rupert but leave the proof for future work.
conclusions: its dual (for any reasonable definition of this term) is locally Rupert

nodes.name: Rhombicosidodecahedron is not Rupert
nodes.statement: In \cite[Conjecture 2]{StYu23} we conjectured that the Rhombicosidodecahedron (\textbf{RID} in short) does not have Rupert's property.
conclusions: the Rhombicosidodecahedron (\textbf{RID} in short) does not have Rupert's property

nodes.name: Rhombicosidodecahedron
nodes.statement: Recall that the Rhombicosidodecahedron can be defined as the set of all even permutations of $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm\Phi^3)$, $(\pm\Phi^2,\pm\Phi,\pm2\Phi)$ and $(\pm(2+\Phi),0,\pm\Phi^2)$ with $\Phi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ the golden ratio.

nodes.name: Other methods to exclude local solutions
nodes.statement: Are there other ways to disprove the existence of local solutions? That is, without the method utilized in \cref{lem:langles} and \cref{thm:local}, or setting up an algebraic system of inequalities.

nodes.name: Proving non-Rupertness without massive subdivision
nodes.statement: Is there a way to prove that a solid does not have Rupert's property without splitting $\mathbb{R}^5$ into millions of small regions and solving each separately?

nodes.name: Proving optimality of Nieuwland numbers
nodes.statement:
Find a method to prove that a solution to Rupert's property is (locally) optimal, i.e. it has the (locally) the largest Nieuwland number. More generally, how to prove the conjectured Nieuwland numbers? It is, for instance, still open to prove that the Octahedron has Nieuwland number $3\sqrt{2}/4$ or that the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron both have Nieuwland number $\nu \approx 1.0108$, a root of
    \(
        P(x) = 2025x^8 - 11970x^6 + 17009x^4 - 9000x^2 + 2000
    \).
nodes.statement_short: Find methods to prove (local) optimality of Rupert solutions, e.g. the conjectured Nieuwland numbers of the octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.

nodes.name: Verification of a global-theorem leaf
nodes.statement_short: For a leaf of type 1, build $w$, $\widetilde S$ and the rational matrices, compute $G^\mathbb{Q}$ and all $H_P^\mathbb{Q}$, and check $G^\mathbb{Q}>\max H_P^\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Verification of a local-theorem leaf
nodes.statement:
Similarly to the global theorem verification after the steps 1. and 2. above, we perform the following steps for each row with nodeType=2:

    \begin{enumerate}
    \setcounter{enumi}{2}
    \item Check that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ and $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are congruent by applying \cref{lem:congruent} (verifying that $P^tP = Q^tQ$ and $\det(Q) \neq 0$).
    \item Compute $\overline{M_1}$, $\overline{M_2} \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 3}$, $\overline{X_1}, \overline{X_2} \in \mathbb{Q}^{3}$ and $R_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}) \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 2}$ as in \cref{thm:global_rational}.
    \item Set $\sigma_Q =$ sigma\_Q and check that 
    \[
        \langle \overline{X_1}, \widetilde{P}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon + 3 \kappa \quad \text{ and } \quad (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2},\widetilde{P}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon +3 \kappa.
    \]
    \item Check that $\widetilde{P}_1,\widetilde{P}_2,\widetilde{P}_3$ are $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $\widetilde{Q}_1,\widetilde{Q}_2,\widetilde{Q}_3$ are $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)$ by verifying the inequalities in \cref{def:ekspanning}:
        \begin{align*}
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_1, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{2}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_2, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{3}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_3, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{1}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,
        \end{align*}
        and 
            \begin{align*}
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_1, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{2}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_2, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{3}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_3, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{1}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa.
        \end{align*}
    \item Set $r = r'/1000 \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r'$ taken from the r column and define
        \[
            \delta = \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_i-\overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i\right\|_{+}/2 + 3\kappa \in \mathbb{Q}.
        \]
    \item Check that $\| \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i \|_{-} > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 3\kappa$ for $i=1,2,3$.
    \item Finally verify that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i,\overline{M_2} (\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\rangle - 10\kappa - 2 \varepsilon ( \|\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j\|_{+} + 2 \kappa ) \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i\|_{+}+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 3\kappa \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\|_{+}+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 6 \kappa\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta}{r},
    \]
    for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $\widetilde{Q}_j \in \widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}} \setminus \widetilde{Q}_i$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a leaf of type 2, check congruence, the (A) inequalities, $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning, the bound on $r$ and the (B) inequalities in rational arithmetic.

nodes.name: Mirror a solution
nodes.statement:
Let us assume a solution $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha)$ to the Rupert condition
    $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P})^\circ$
    is given. Then, this inclusion still holds true, when mirroring all the points along the $x$-axis, hence
    $$\begin{pmatrix} 
        1&0\\
        0&-1
    \end{pmatrix}
    R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)\mathbf{P} \subset \begin{pmatrix} 
        1&0\\
        0&-1
    \end{pmatrix}(M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P})^\circ.$$
nodes.statement_short: Assume a solution and mirror the inclusion along the $x$-axis.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron

nodes.name: Apply the reflection identity
nodes.statement:
Using 
    \[
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            1&0\\
            0&-1
        \end{pmatrix}R(\alpha)=
        R({-\alpha})\begin{pmatrix} 
            1&0\\
            0&-1
        \end{pmatrix}
    \]
    and the third identity in \cref{lem:symmetries}, we arrive at
    \[
        R({-\alpha})M({\theta_1+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_1}) \mathbf{P}
        \subset (M({\theta_2+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_2})\mathbf{P})^\circ.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Commute the reflection with $R(\alpha)$ and apply the third symmetry identity.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron

nodes.name: Reduce phi_2
nodes.statement:
So, if $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha)$ is a solution to Rupert's condition for $\mathbf{P}$, then 
    \[
        (\theta_1+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_1,\theta_2+\pi/15,\pi-\varphi_2,-\alpha)
    \]
    is also a solution. It follows that we may assume that there exists a solution with $\varphi_2\in[0,\pi/2]$.
nodes.statement_short: The transformed parameters are again a solution, so $\varphi_2\le\pi/2$ may be assumed.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron

nodes.name: Reduce remaining parameters
nodes.statement: Finally, using the first and second identity of \cref{lem:symmetries}, we can enforce the remaining parameters to lie in the claimed intervals.
nodes.statement_short: The other two symmetries reduce $\theta_i$ and $\alpha$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Refined Rupert's property for the Noperthedron

nodes.name: Reduce to 2D rotation
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\|R_x(\alpha)-R_x(\bar\alpha)\|$ and identify it with the 2D rotation difference.

nodes.name: Arc versus chord
nodes.statement: For the inequality we first observe that for any $v\in\mathbb{R}^2$ the points $R(\alpha)v$ and $R(\overline{\alpha})v$ lie on the circle with radius $\|v\|$. The length of the arc connecting them has length at most $|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\cdot \|v\|$ and is always longer than the straight line connecting them with length $\|R(\alpha)v-R(\overline{\alpha})v\|$.
nodes.statement_short: The chord between $R(\alpha)v$ and $R(\bar\alpha)v$ is shorter than the arc of length $|\alpha-\bar\alpha|\|v\|$.

nodes.name: Conclude the bound
nodes.statement:
Hence we~have  
    \[
        \|R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha})\|=\max_{v\in\mathbb{R}^2} \frac{\|(R(\alpha)-R(\overline{\alpha}))v\|}{\|v\|} < \max_{v\in\mathbb{R}^2} \frac{|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\cdot \|v\|}{\|v\|}=|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|\leq \varepsilon. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Take the maximum over $v$.

nodes.name: Half-angle reduction
nodes.statement:
Using $1+ \cos(x) = 2 \cos(x/2)^2$ three times the inequality becomes equivalent to 
    \[
        \cos(a/2)^2 \cos(b/2)^2 \geq \cos(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}/2)^2.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with $1+\cos x=2\cos^2(x/2)$.

nodes.name: WLOG and product-to-sum
nodes.statement:
Note that without loss of generality we can assume that $0 \leq a, b \leq 2$; let $x=a/2$ and $y=b/2$ so that $0 \leq x,y\leq 1$. Then we need to prove that 
    \[
        \cos(x) \cos(y) \geq \cos(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}),
    \]
    Or, equivalently, 
    \[
        \frac{\cos(x+y) + \cos(x-y)}{2} \geq \cos(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}),
    \]
    as $2 \cos(x) \cos(y) = \cos(x+y) + \cos(x-y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $0\le a,b\le2$, substitute $x=a/2$, $y=b/2$, and use the product-to-sum formula.

nodes.name: Convexity of cos(sqrt t)
nodes.statement:
Now the crucial observation is that $f(t) \coloneqq \cos(\sqrt{t})$ is \emph{convex} for $t \in [0,4]$. Indeed, 
    \[
        f''(t) = \frac{\sin(\sqrt{t}) - \sqrt{t} \cos(\sqrt{t})}{4 \sqrt{t^3}},
    \]
    and $f''(t) \geq 0$ on $t \in [0,4]$ is equivalent to $\sin(s) - s \cos(s) \geq 0$ on $s \in [0,2]$.
nodes.statement_short: $f(t)=\cos\sqrt t$ is convex on $[0,4]$.

nodes.name: Apply Jensen
nodes.statement_short: Jensen's inequality for $f$ at $(x\pm y)^2$ gives the claim.

nodes.name: Equality case
nodes.statement: Equality can only happen for $(x + y)^2 = (x - y)^2$, i.e. $xy=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality forces $xy=0$.

nodes.name: Reduce to small angles
nodes.statement_short: Doubling argument reduces to $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le2$.

nodes.name: Write T as a conjugated rotation
nodes.statement:
Define $T\coloneqq R_x(\alpha)R_y(\beta)$. As $T$ is the composition of two rotation matrices, it is itself a rotation matrix. Therefore $T$ is of the form 
    \[
        T= UR_x(\Psi)U^{-1}
    \]
    for some orthogonal matrix $U$ and $-\pi \leq \Psi \leq \pi$.
nodes.statement_short: $T=R_xR_y$ is a rotation, so $T=UR_x(\Psi)U^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Compare traces
nodes.statement:
We therefore have
    \begin{align*}
    &\text{tr}(R_x(\alpha)R_y(\beta))=\text{tr}(T)=\text{tr}(UR_x(\Psi)U^{-1})=\text{tr}(R_x(\Psi)).
    \end{align*}
It follows that
\[
    \cos(\alpha)+\cos(\beta)+\cos(\alpha)\cos(\beta)=1+2\cos(\Psi),
\]
which is trivially equivalent to $(1+\cos(\alpha))(1+\cos(\beta)) =  2+2\cos(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Comparing traces gives $(1+\cos\alpha)(1+\cos\beta)=2+2\cos\Psi$.

nodes.name: Apply the Jensen-type inequality
nodes.statement:
As $|\alpha|,|\beta| \leq 2$, we can bound the left-hand-side from below using \cref{lem:jensen}: 
\begin{align*}
    2+2\cos\Big(\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\Big)&\leq 2+2\cos(\Psi),
\end{align*}
thus $\cos\Big(\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\Big) \leq \cos(\Psi)$. Since $\sqrt{2\cdot 2^2} = \sqrt{8} < 3$ the arguments of the cosines are between $-\pi$ and $\pi$ and we can conclude that
\(
    \sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\geq |\Psi|.
\)
nodes.statement_short: The Jensen-type lemma yields $|\Psi|\le\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}$.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equalities and the rotation difference bound give the result, with strictness.

nodes.name: Trivial case and factorization
nodes.statement:
For $(\theta, \varphi) = (\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$ the result is trivial since $\varepsilon>0$. In the other case,
    recall the identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR2})
    \[
    M(\theta, \varphi) =
        \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix}
        \cdot R_y(\varphi) \cdot R_z(-\theta),
    \]
    and denote by $Z$ the $2 \times 3$ matrix on the rind-hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of the equal case; otherwise factor $M$ via identity (XMRfromR2).

nodes.name: Reduce to a rotation product
nodes.statement_short: Sub-multiplicativity and orthogonality reduce to $\|\mathrm{Id}-R_yR_z\|$.

nodes.name: Apply rotation product bound
nodes.statement: The right-hand side is strictly smaller than $\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2 + (\varphi-\overline{\varphi})^2} \leq \sqrt{2}\varepsilon$ by \cref{lem:RxRy} using that $(\theta, \varphi) \neq (\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$.
nodes.statement_short: The rotation product lemma gives $<\sqrt2\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Analogous case for X
nodes.statement: The proof for $\|X({\theta, \varphi})-X(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\|$ is analogous using the corresponding identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR1})    for $X({\theta, \varphi})$.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument with identity (XMRfromR1).

nodes.name: Factor through axis rotations
nodes.statement:
Recall the identity (\ref{eq:XMRfromR3})
    \[
    R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)=
       \begin{pmatrix} 
            0 & 1 & 0\\ 
            -1 & 0 & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix}
        R_z(\alpha) \cdot R_y(\varphi) \cdot R_z(-\theta)
    \] 
    to obtain like in the proof of \cref{lem:sqrt2}:
    \begin{align*}
        \|R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)-R(\overline{\alpha})M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| \leq \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi) - R_y(\overline{\varphi}) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|
    \end{align*}
    using the sub-multiplicativity of the norm.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\|R_z(\alpha-\bar\alpha)R_y(\varphi)-R_y(\bar\varphi)R_z(\theta-\bar\theta)\|$.

nodes.name: Interpolating angle Phi
nodes.statement:
Now define   
    \[
        \Phi = \frac{\varphi\cdot |\theta-\overline{\theta}| +\overline{\varphi}\cdot |\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|}{|\alpha-\overline{\alpha}|+|\theta-\overline{\theta}|},
    \]
    and obtain further using the triangle inequality and \cref{lem:RxRy}:
    \begin{align*}
        \|R(\alpha) M(\theta, \varphi)-R(\overline{\alpha})M(\overline{\theta},\overline{\varphi})\| 
        &\leq \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi) - R_y(\Phi)\|+ \|R_y(\Phi)-R_y(\overline{\varphi}) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|\\
        &= \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha}) \cdot R_y(\varphi-\Phi) - \text{Id}\|+ \|\text{Id}-R_y(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi) \cdot R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|\\
        &\leq \sqrt{(\alpha-\overline{\alpha})^2+(\varphi-\Phi)^2}+\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2+(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi)^2}.
    \end{align*}
    Note that also by \cref{lem:RxRy} this inequality is strict except if both sides vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Insert $R_y(\Phi)$ and apply the rotation product bound to both terms.

nodes.name: Evaluate the bound
nodes.statement:
The definition of $\Phi$ conveniently implies after a small computation that 
    \[
        \sqrt{(\alpha-\overline{\alpha})^2+(\varphi-\Phi)^2}+\sqrt{(\theta-\overline{\theta})^2+(\overline{\varphi}-\Phi)^2} = \sqrt{\left(|\alpha - \overline{\alpha}|+|\theta - \overline{\theta}|\right)^2 + |\varphi-\overline{\varphi}|^2} \leq \sqrt{5}\varepsilon,
    \]
    which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The choice of $\Phi$ makes the sum equal $\sqrt{(|\Delta\alpha|+|\Delta\theta|)^2+|\Delta\varphi|^2}\le\sqrt5\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Convex combination
nodes.statement: Write $S = \sum_i \lambda_i P_i$ for $P_i \in \mathcal{P}$ the vertices of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\lambda_i \in [0,1)$ such that $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$. Moreover, denote $M \coloneqq \max_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \langle P ,w\rangle $.
nodes.statement_short: Write $S$ as a convex combination of vertices and name the maximum $M$.

nodes.name: Linearity
nodes.statement:
Then:
    \[
        \langle S ,w \rangle = \sum_i \lambda_i \langle P_i, w \rangle \leq M \cdot \sum_i \lambda_i = M. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of the scalar product gives the bound.

nodes.name: Restrict to a segment
nodes.statement:
Let $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $y = (y_1,\dots,y_n)$. We define $g:[0,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ by
    \[
        g(t) = f\big(x_1(1-t)+y_1t, \dots ,x_n(1-t)+y_nt\big) = f(x(1-t)+yt)
    \]
    and observe that 
    \[
        g(1)-g(0)=\int_0^1g'(t)\text{d}t=\int_0^1\int_0^t g''(s)\text{d}s+g'(0)\text{d}t=g'(0)+\int_0^1\int_0^t g''(s)\text{d}s\text{d}t.
    \]
    Note that $|g(1)-g(0)|$ is exactly the term which needs to be bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Define $g(t)=f(x(1-t)+yt)$ and express $g(1)-g(0)$ through $g'(0)$ and $g''$.

nodes.name: First derivative bound
nodes.statement:
The chain rule implies that 
    \[
        g'(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-x_i) \partial_{x_i} f(x(1-t)+yt),
    \]
    thus at $t=0$ we find
    \begin{align*}
    |g'(0)| \leq\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i-x_i| \cdot | \partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)| \leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^n |\partial_{x_i} f(x_1,\dots,x_n)|. 
    \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|g'(0)|$ by $\varepsilon\sum|\partial_i f|$.

nodes.name: Second derivative bound
nodes.statement:
For the second derivative of $g(t)$ we also get with the chain rule
    $$g''(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n(y_i-x_i)(y_j-x_j) \cdot \partial_{x_i} \partial_{x_j} f\big(x(1-t)+y t\big),$$
   which implies that
    $|g''(t)|\leq n^2 \varepsilon^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|g''|\le n^2\varepsilon^2$.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the bounds.

nodes.name: Assume a solution in U
nodes.statement: We prove the statement by contradiction: Assume that there exists $S \in \mathbf{P}$ with a unit vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^2$ like in the assumption and $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in U$ such that Rupert's condition is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a solution exists in $U$.

nodes.name: Apply the hull scalar-product lemma
nodes.statement:
As noted before, Rupert's condition and \cref{lem:hullscalarprod} imply in particular that 
    \[
        \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)P,w \rangle < \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Rupert's condition bounds the max scalar product of the inner projection strictly.

nodes.name: Chain of inequalities
nodes.statement:
We shall, however, show that the following sequence of inequalities yields the desired contradiction: 
    \[
        \max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)P,w \rangle \stackrel{\text{(i)}}{\geq} \langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S,w \rangle\stackrel{\text{(ii)}}{\geq} G \stackrel{\text{(iii)}}{>}H\stackrel{\text{(iv)}}{\geq}\max_{P\in \mathbf{P}}\langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle.
    \]

    
    The inequality (i) is obvious and (iii) is an assumption of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: State the contradicting chain (i)-(iv); (i) is obvious, (iii) is assumed.

nodes.name: Prove inequality (ii)
nodes.statement:
To show inequality (ii) define the function 
    \[
        f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S/\|S\|,w \rangle = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S,w \rangle/\|S\|.
    \]
    Then \cref{lem:leq1} guarantees that 
    \[
        \left|\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq 1,
    \]
    for all $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ and any $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$; therefore \cref{lem:n2} applies and implies that
    \[
        |f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})-f(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\alpha)|\leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^3 |\partial_{x_i} f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})| + \frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^2,
    \]
    as $|\overline{\theta}_1-\theta_1|,|\overline{\varphi}_1-\varphi_1|,|\overline{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq \varepsilon$ by assumption. Multiplying the inequality with $\|S\|$ we get
    \begin{align*}
        |\langle R(a)  M({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle-\langle R(\alpha) M(\theta_1, \varphi_1)S,w \rangle| & \\
       & \hspace{-6.5cm} \leq \varepsilon\cdot\bigg(|\langle R(\alpha)  M({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha})  M^\theta({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|+|\langle R(\overline{\alpha})  M^\varphi({\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1})S,w \rangle|\bigg) +\frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^2\|S\|.
    \end{align*}
    From this and $\|S\|\leq 1$ the inequality (ii) follows.
nodes.statement_short: Second-order Taylor bound for $f$ at the centre gives (ii).

nodes.name: Define f
nodes.statement:
To show inequality (ii) define the function 
    \[
        f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S/\|S\|,w \rangle = \langle R({x_3}) M({x_1,x_2})S,w \rangle/\|S\|.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Normalized scalar product as function of $(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Apply Hessian and Taylor bounds
nodes.statement:
Then \cref{lem:leq1} guarantees that 
    \[
        \left|\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq 1,
    \]
    for all $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ and any $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$; therefore \cref{lem:n2} applies and implies that
    \[
        |f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})-f(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\alpha)|\leq \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^3 |\partial_{x_i} f(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\alpha})| + \frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^2,
    \]
    as $|\overline{\theta}_1-\theta_1|,|\overline{\varphi}_1-\varphi_1|,|\overline{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq \varepsilon$ by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Hessian entries at most 1, so the Taylor bound applies.

nodes.name: Rescale
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $\|S\|\le1$ to obtain (ii).

nodes.name: Prove inequality (iv)
nodes.statement:
Finally, inequality (iv) can be shown in a similar way: for every $P \in \mathbf{P}$, again using \cref{lem:n2}, it holds that
    \[ 
        \langle   M({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle + \varepsilon\cdot\bigg(|\langle M^\theta({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle|+|\langle  M^\varphi({\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2})P,w \rangle|\bigg)+ 2\varepsilon^2 \geq \langle  M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)P,w \rangle. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: The Taylor bound for each $P$ gives (iv).

nodes.name: Orthogonal stacked matrix
nodes.statement:
Define the matrix 
    \[
        A({\theta,\varphi}) \coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}
        M(\theta, \varphi)\\
        X({\theta,\varphi})^t
        \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}.
    \]
    Note that $A({\theta,\varphi}) \cdot A({\theta,\varphi})^t = \mathrm{Id}$, thus the matrix is orthogonal and hence it is length-preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Stack $M$ and $X^t$ into an orthogonal matrix $A$.

nodes.name: Length preservation
nodes.statement:
We therefore obtain
    \[
        \|P\|^2=\|A({\theta,\varphi})P\|^2=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}
        M(\theta, \varphi)P\\
        \langle X({\theta, \varphi}),P\rangle
        \end{pmatrix}\right\|^2=\big\|M(\theta, \varphi) P\big\|^2+\langle X({\theta, \varphi}),P\rangle^2. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Norm preservation gives the identity.

nodes.name: Assume all inequalities
nodes.statement:
Let $V = (V_1|V_2|V_3) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ and assume by contradiction that all inequalities hold. This translates into
\begin{align} V^T Y \gg V^T Z,
\end{align}
where we use $x \gg y$ for vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^3$ if $x_1>y_1,x_2>y_2$ and $x_3>y_3.$
nodes.statement_short: Assume all three inequalities, i.e. $V^TY\gg V^TZ$.

nodes.name: Positive weights
nodes.statement:
Moreover, let $\lambda, 
u \in \mathbb{R}^3_{>0}$ such that $Y = \lambda_1 V_1+\lambda_2V_2+\lambda_3V_3$ and
$Z = 
u_1 V_1+
u_2V_2+
u_3V_3$. In other words, we have 
\[
Y =  V \lambda  \quad 	ext{ and }  \quad Z =  V
u .
\]
nodes.statement_short: Write $Y=V\lambda$, $Z=V\nu$ with positive weights.

nodes.name: Translate hypotheses
nodes.statement:
The assumption that $\|Y\| = \|Z\|$ translates therefore into
\[
\lambda^T V^T V \lambda = \nu^T V^T V \nu,
\]
and the inequalities $(\ref{ineq})$ rewrite as
\[
V^T V \lambda \gg V^T V \nu.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the norm equality and inequalities through $V^TV$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement:
Using this and the positivity of $\lambda,
u \in \mathbb{R}^3$, we find a contradiction in 
\[
    \lambda^T V^T V \lambda > \lambda^T V^T V 
u = (
u^T V^T V \lambda)^T > (
u^TV^TV
u)^T = \lambda^T V^T V \lambda.  \qedhere
\]
nodes.statement_short: Positivity gives a strict chain from a quantity to itself.

nodes.name: Reuse the previous proof
nodes.statement_short: The previous argument gives a bound with $2\|B\|$.

nodes.name: Symmetrize
nodes.statement: Exchanging $A$ and $B$, however, also gives the same inequality with $2\|A\|$ instead of $2\|B\|$. Taking the arithmetic mean of these two upper bounds produces the desired symmetric inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Swap $A,B$ and average the two bounds.

nodes.name: Coordinate vectors and cross product
nodes.statement: Write $A=(A_1,A_2)^t$, $B=(B_1,B_2)^t$, $C=(C_1,C_2)^t$ and consider the two vectors $v_1=(A_1,B_1,C_1)^t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $v_2=(A_2,B_2,C_2)^t \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Now set $(a,b,c)^t \coloneqq v_1\times v_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to be the cross product of $v_1$ and $v_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Form $v_1,v_2$ from coordinates and set $(a,b,c)=v_1\times v_2$.

nodes.name: Weights annihilate
nodes.statement:
By the orthogonality property of the cross product we obtain
    \[
        aA+bB+cC=\big(A| B| C\big)\cdot (v_1\times v_2)=\begin{pmatrix}
            v_1^t\\ v_2^t
        \end{pmatrix} (v_1\times v_2)=\begin{pmatrix}
            0\\0
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality of the cross product gives $aA+bB+cC=0$.

nodes.name: Weights are positive
nodes.statement:
Additionally observe that
    \[
        \begin{pmatrix}
            a\\b\\c
        \end{pmatrix}= v_1\times v_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
            A_1\\B_1\\C_1
        \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}
            A_2\\B_2\\C_2
        \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}
            B_1C_2-C_1B_2\\C_1A_2-A_1C_2\\A_1B_2-B_1A_2
        \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}
            \langle R(\pi/2) B,C\rangle\\
            \langle R(\pi/2) C,A\rangle\\
            \langle R(\pi/2) A,B\rangle
        \end{pmatrix},
    \]
    thus $a,b,c >0$.
nodes.statement_short: The weights equal the three positive cross-product quantities.

nodes.name: Spanning survives perturbation
nodes.statement:
It follows from the definition of $\varepsilon$-spanning and \cref{lem:sqrt2} that 
    \begin{align} \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_1,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{2}\rangle > 0, \nonumber \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_2,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{3}\rangle > 0, \\
        \langle R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi) P_3,M(\theta, \varphi) P_{1}\rangle > 0, \nonumber
    \end{align}
    using \cref{lem:scalarprodbars} on $A=R(\pi/2) M(\theta, \varphi), B =  M(\theta, \varphi)$ analogously for $\overline{A}, \overline{B}$ with the fact that $\|R(\pi/2)\|=1$ and $\|P_1\|,\|P_2\|,\|P_3\| \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The scalar product bound and $\sqrt2\varepsilon$ bound keep the three cross products positive.

nodes.name: Origin inside projected triangle
nodes.statement:
Thus, \cref{lem:origintriangle} implies that the origin $O$ is strictly inside the triangle $\Delta(M(\theta, \varphi) P_1, M(\theta, \varphi) P_2, M(\theta, \varphi) P_3)$.
    It follows that there exist $a,b,c >0$ such~that 
    \begin{align} aM(\theta,\varphi)P_1 + bM(\theta,\varphi)P_2 + cM(\theta,\varphi)P_3 = O.
    \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The origin-in-triangle criterion yields positive $a,b,c$ with vanishing projected combination.

nodes.name: Kernel argument
nodes.statement: Consider the point $S = aP_1 + bP_2 + cP_3\in \mathbb{R}^3$. From (\ref{eq:Ybarkernel}) it follows that $S \in \ker M(\theta,\varphi)$. However, since $X \coloneqq X(\theta, \varphi) \in \ker M(\theta,\varphi)$ as well, we get that $S = \lambda X(\theta, \varphi)$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: $S=aP_1+bP_2+cP_3$ lies in $\ker M$, hence is a multiple of $X$.

nodes.name: Positive multiple
nodes.statement:
It follows that
    \[
        \lambda = \langle X, \lambda X \rangle = \langle X, S \rangle = a \langle X, P_1\rangle + b \langle X, P_2\rangle + c \langle X, P_3\rangle > 0,
    \]
    and, consequently, that $X(\theta, \varphi) = \frac{1}{\lambda}S \in \mathrm{span}^+(P_1, P_2, P_3)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda>0$ since each $\langle X,P_i\rangle>0$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let $A \in \mathrm{Sect}_\delta(\overline{Q}) = \mathrm{Disc}_\delta(\overline{Q}) \cap \mathcal{P}^\circ$. We need to show that $\|A\| < \|Q\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $A$ in the sector; show $\|A\|<\|Q\|$.

nodes.name: Cosine theorem
nodes.statement:
By the cosine theorem in the triangle $\Delta OQA$ it holds that 
    \[
        \| A \|^2 = \|Q\|^2 + \|Q - A\|^2 - 2\|Q\|\|Q - A\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)).
    \]
    Or, equivalently, that 
    \[
        \|A\|^2 - \|Q\|^2 = \|Q - A\| \cdot (\|Q - A\| - 2\|Q\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A))).
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $\|A\|^2-\|Q\|^2$ by the cosine theorem.

nodes.name: Angle bound
nodes.statement:
Now observe that $\angle(O,Q,A) < \angle(O,Q,P_j)$ for some vertex $P_j \in \mathcal{P} \setminus Q$ because $A \in \mathcal{P}^\circ$. Moreover, recall that 
    \[
    \cos(\angle(O,Q,P_j)) = \frac{\langle Q, Q - P_j \rangle}{\|Q\|\|Q - P_j\|} \geq \delta/r,
    \]
    thus $\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)) \geq \delta/r$.
nodes.statement_short: Convexity bounds the angle at $Q$ by one at a neighbouring vertex.

nodes.name: Length bounds
nodes.statement: We also have that $\|Q\| \geq r$ by assumption and $\|Q - A\| < 2\delta$ because both $Q, A \in \mathrm{Disc}_\delta(\overline{Q})$.
nodes.statement_short: $\|Q\|\ge r$ and $\|Q-A\|<2\delta$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
We conclude that 
    \[
        \|Q - A\| - 2\|Q\|\cos(\angle(O,Q,A)) < 2\delta - 2r\cdot\delta/r = 0,
    \]
    therefore $\|A\|^2 - \|Q\|^2 < 0$ and $\|A\| < \|Q\|$
nodes.statement_short: The factor is negative, so $\|A\|<\|Q\|$.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We will show that the numerator of the left-hand side is bigger than the one of the right-hand side, and that the factors in the denominator are smaller. We also show that the left-hand side is well-defined as $MP, M(P-Q) \neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare numerators and denominators separately.

nodes.name: Numerator bound
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric scalar-product bound with $\|M-\bar M\|<\sqrt2\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: First denominator factor
nodes.statement:
For the first factor in the denominator we simply have 
\[
\| \overline{M} P \| \geq \| M P \| - \| MP - \overline{M}P \| \geq \| M P \| - \| M - \overline{M} \| \cdot \|P\| \geq \|MP\| - \sqrt{2} \varepsilon,
\]
with the triangle inequality and \cref{lem:sqrt2}.
nodes.statement_short: $\|\bar MP\|\ge\|MP\|-\sqrt2\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Second denominator factor
nodes.statement:
For the other factor we obtain similarly 
\[
\| \overline{M} (P-Q) \| \geq \| M (P-Q) \| - \| M - \overline{M} \| \cdot \|P-Q\| \geq \|M(P-Q)\| - 2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon,
\]
using that $\|P-Q\| \leq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: $\|\bar M(P-Q)\|\ge\|M(P-Q)\|-2\sqrt2\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: If $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent then $\langle P_i,P_j\rangle = \langle LQ_i,LQ_j\rangle = \langle Q_i,Q_j\rangle$, thus $P^t P = Q^t Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormal maps preserve inner products.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement:
For the other direction, we claim that $L \coloneqq PQ^{-1}$ is orthonormal and satisfies that $P_i = LQ_i$ for all $i=1,2,3$.  
    Indeed,  $L^t L = (PQ^{-1})^t (PQ^{-1}) = (Q^t)^{-1} P^t P Q^{-1} = \mathrm{Id}$ and it holds that $LQ=PQ^{-1}Q=P$, thus $LQ_i = P_i$.
nodes.statement_short: $L=PQ^{-1}$ satisfies $L^tL=\mathrm{Id}$ and $LQ=P$.

nodes.name: Assume a solution; set up Y, Z
nodes.statement: Assume by contradiction that there exists a $\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha) \in U$ which solves Rupert's problem. By assumption $(P_1,P_2,P_3)$ and $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)$ are congruent, thus there exists an orthonormal matrix $L \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ with $P_i  = LQ_i$ for all $i=1,2,3$. Set $Y \coloneqq X(\theta_1, \varphi_1)$ and $Z \coloneqq K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2)$, where $K \coloneqq (-1)^{\sigma_P + \sigma_Q}L$, so it is easy to see that $\|Y\|=\|Z\|=1$. Moreover, let $\overline{P_i} = (-1)^{\sigma_P} P_i$ and $\overline{Q_i} = (-1)^{\sigma_Q} Q_i$, so that $\overline{P_i} = K\overline{Q_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a solution in $U$, take the orthonormal $L$, and define $Y$, $Z$, $\bar P_i$, $\bar Q_i$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Reduce to the scalar products lemma
nodes.statement:
We shall show that 
        \begin{align} Y,Z \in \mathrm{span}^+(\overline{P_1},\overline{P_2},\overline{P_3})
        \end{align}
        and that
        \begin{align} \langle Y, \overline{P_i} \rangle > \langle Z, \overline{P_i} \rangle \text{ for each } i=1,2,3,
        \end{align}
        then \cref{lem:langles} yields the desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove (YZinspanp) and (angles), then apply the scalar products lemma.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Y and Z in the positive cone
nodes.statement:
First observe that (A$_\varepsilon$) and \cref{lem:XP>0} imply that
    \begin{equation} \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle, \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle > 0.
    \end{equation}
    Now (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) for $Y = X(\theta_1, \varphi_1)$ follows from \cref{lem:eps-spanning}. By the same argument we also get that 
    \[
        X(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \in \mathrm{span}^+(\overline{Q_1},\overline{Q_2},\overline{Q_3}).
    \]
    However, then (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) also immediately follows for $Z = K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2)$ as $\overline{P_i} = K \overline{Q_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (YZinspanp) via the positivity and $\varepsilon$-spanning lemmas.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Points in front
nodes.statement_short: (A$_\varepsilon$) gives positive scalar products after perturbation.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Y in cone
nodes.statement: Now (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) for $Y = X(\theta_1, \varphi_1)$ follows from \cref{lem:eps-spanning}.
nodes.statement_short: The $\varepsilon$-spanning lemma gives $Y$ in the cone.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Z in cone
nodes.statement:
By the same argument we also get that 
    \[
        X(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \in \mathrm{span}^+(\overline{Q_1},\overline{Q_2},\overline{Q_3}).
    \]
    However, then (\ref{eq:YZinspanp_fin}) also immediately follows for $Z = K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2)$ as $\overline{P_i} = K \overline{Q_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Same for $X(\theta_2,\varphi_2)$, transported by $K$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Q_i are locally maximally distant
nodes.statement:
We proceed with proving (\ref{eq:angles_fin}). First note that by assumption $\| \overline{M_2} Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon$, thus  \cref{lem:MP>r} shows that 
    \(
        \| M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \| > r.
    \)
    Define 
    \[
        T_i \coloneqq \left(R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} P_i + \overline{M_2} Q_i\right)/2 \in \mathbb{R}^2,
    \]
    for $i=1,2,3$ so that by assumption $\|T_i - \overline{M_2} Q_i\| \leq \delta$. Then also set
    \[
        \mathrm{Disc}_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon}(T_i) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^2: \| x - T_i \| < \delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon \}.
    \] 
    By \cref{lem:inCirc} it holds that $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1, \varphi_2) P_i, M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i$.
    Moreover, as the right-hand side in (B$_\varepsilon$) is positive, \cref{lem:coss} implies that 
    \[
    \frac{\langle M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i,M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle}{\|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i\| \cdot \|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)(Q_i-Q_j)\|} \geq 
    \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} Q_i,\overline{M_2} (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)},
    \]
    Thus, using assumption (B$_\varepsilon$), the left-hand side of this inequality is also larger than $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon)/r$. \cref{lem:LMD} now implies that $M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P}$ is $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon$)-LMD with respect to $T_i$. We obtain that for any $A \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ it holds that $\|A\| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the projected $Q_i$ are LMD in the disc around $T_i$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Norm lower bound
nodes.statement:
We proceed with proving (\ref{eq:angles_fin}). First note that by assumption $\| \overline{M_2} Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon$, thus  \cref{lem:MP>r} shows that 
    \(
        \| M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \| > r.
    \)
nodes.statement_short: Projection norm lower bound gives $\|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|>r$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Midpoints and discs
nodes.statement:
Define 
    \[
        T_i \coloneqq \left(R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} P_i + \overline{M_2} Q_i\right)/2 \in \mathbb{R}^2,
    \]
    for $i=1,2,3$ so that by assumption $\|T_i - \overline{M_2} Q_i\| \leq \delta$. Then also set
    \[
        \mathrm{Disc}_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Disc}_{\delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon}(T_i) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^2: \| x - T_i \| < \delta + \sqrt{5} \varepsilon \}.
    \] 
    By \cref{lem:inCirc} it holds that $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1, \varphi_2) P_i, M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Define midpoints $T_i$ and discs; both perturbed points lie in them by the disc lemma.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Cosine bound
nodes.statement:
Moreover, as the right-hand side in (B$_\varepsilon$) is positive, \cref{lem:coss} implies that 
    \[
    \frac{\langle M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i,M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle}{\|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i\| \cdot \|M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)(Q_i-Q_j)\|} \geq 
    \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} Q_i,\overline{M_2} (Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \varepsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)},
    \]
    Thus, using assumption (B$_\varepsilon$), the left-hand side of this inequality is also larger than $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon)/r$.
nodes.statement_short: The cosine perturbation bound and (B$_\varepsilon$) give the angle condition.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Apply LMD criterion
nodes.statement: \cref{lem:LMD} now implies that $M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) Q_i \in M(\theta_2, \varphi_2)\mathbf{P}$ is $(\delta + \sqrt{5}\varepsilon$)-LMD with respect to $T_i$. We obtain that for any $A \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ it holds that $\|A\| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$.
nodes.statement_short: The acute-angle criterion makes $M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i$ LMD.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Derive the decrease and conclude
nodes.statement:
Recall that by contradiction we assumed that $\Psi$ is a solution to Rupert's problem, thus, in particular, $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ and it follows that $A = R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$.
    We conclude that $ \| M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$. Now \cref{lem:pythagoras} implies that $ \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), P_i \rangle^2 > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), Q_i \rangle^2$ and (\ref{eq:YPiZPi>0_fin}) implies that 
    \[
        \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle.
    \]
    We conclude that (\ref{eq:angles_fin}) holds because
    \[
        \langle Y, \overline{P_i} \rangle = \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle>
        \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), K\overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle Z, \overline{P_i} \rangle. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Rupert's condition places the inner points in the disc, so their norms are smaller; Pythagoras turns this into (angles).
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Norms decrease
nodes.statement:
Recall that by contradiction we assumed that $\Psi$ is a solution to Rupert's problem, thus, in particular, $R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$ and it follows that $A = R(\alpha)M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \in \mathrm{Disc}_i \cap (M(\theta_2, \varphi_2) \mathbf{P})^\circ$.
    We conclude that $ \| M(\theta_1,\varphi_1)P_i \| < \|M(\theta_2,\varphi_2)Q_i\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Inner projected points lie in the disc and interior, hence have smaller norm.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Pythagoras
nodes.statement:
Now \cref{lem:pythagoras} implies that $ \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), P_i \rangle^2 > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), Q_i \rangle^2$ and (\ref{eq:YPiZPi>0_fin}) implies that 
    \[
        \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle > \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Smaller projection norm means larger scalar product with the direction.
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Transport by K
nodes.statement:
We conclude that (\ref{eq:angles_fin}) holds because
    \[
        \langle Y, \overline{P_i} \rangle = \langle X(\theta_1, \varphi_1), \overline{P_i} \rangle>
        \langle X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), \overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle K X(\theta_2, \varphi_2), K\overline{Q_i} \rangle
        = 
        \langle Z, \overline{P_i} \rangle. \qedhere
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Transport by the orthonormal $K$ gives (angles).
nodes.section: 5.2 Statement and proof of the local theorem

nodes.name: Entrywise bound
nodes.statement_short: Each entry error is below $\kappa/3$.

nodes.name: Apply entrywise norm bound
nodes.statement: So we can apply \cref{lem:A<deltamn} and obtain that $\|A(x,y)-A_{\mathbb{Q}}(x,y)\|<\kappa/3\cdot \sqrt{3\cdot 3}=\kappa$.
nodes.statement_short: Norm at most $\kappa$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the statement by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ the inequality $\|A_1-B_1\|\leq \kappa \delta_1$ is true since $\|A_1-B_1\|\leq \kappa$ and $\delta_1\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; the case $n=1$ is immediate.

nodes.name: Telescoping step
nodes.statement:
Now let $\alpha_n \coloneqq \|A_1\cdots A_n-B_1\cdots B_n\|$. We find, using the triangle inequality, submultiplicativity of the norm and $\|A_i\|,\|B_i\| \leq \delta_i$ that
    \[
        \alpha_{n} \leq \| A_1 \cdots A_{n-1} \| \cdot \| A_{n} - B_{n} \| + \alpha_{n-1} \cdot \|B_{n}\| \leq \delta_1 \cdots \delta_{n-1} \cdot \kappa + \alpha_{n-1} \cdot \delta_{n}.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality bounds $\alpha_n$ by $\delta_1\cdots\delta_{n-1}\kappa+\alpha_{n-1}\delta_n$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
By induction it holds that $\alpha_{n-1} \leq (n-1)\kappa \cdot \delta_1\cdots \delta_{n-1} $, thus we obtain that 
    \[
        \alpha_{n} \leq \delta_1 \cdots \delta_{n-1} \cdot \kappa + (n-1)\kappa \cdot \delta_1\cdots \delta_{n-1} \cdot \delta_{n} = \kappa \cdot \delta_1\cdots \delta_{n-1} \cdot (1 + (n-1) \delta_n) \leq n\kappa \cdot \delta_1\cdots \delta_n,
    \]
    using that $1 + (n-1) \delta_n \leq n\delta_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Insert the induction hypothesis.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: The proof is a direct application of \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn}. We will only show (\ref{eq:boundskappa1}) and (\ref{eq:boundskappa4}) as the other inequalities are proven in a completely analogous way.
nodes.statement_short: Only (1) and (4) are shown.

nodes.name: Bound (1)
nodes.statement:
Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we obtain
    \[
        | \langle M P, w\rangle - \langle M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}, w\rangle | = | \langle M P - M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}, w\rangle | \leq \| MP - M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P} \| \cdot \|w\|.
    \]
    Now observe that $\|w\|=1$ and $\| MP - M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P} \| \leq 2 \kappa (1+\kappa)^2$ by \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn} since $\|M_{\mathbb{Q}}\|, \|\widetilde{P}\| \leq 1 + \kappa$ by \cref{corr:kappa1kappa}. Then (\ref{eq:boundskappa1}) follows because $(1+\kappa)^2 < 3/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz and the product bound with two factors.

nodes.name: Bound (4)
nodes.statement:
For (\ref{eq:boundskappa4}) it follows in the same way that 
    \[
        | \langle R M P, w\rangle - \langle R_{\mathbb{Q}} M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}, w\rangle | \leq \|R M P - R_{\mathbb{Q}} M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}\| \cdot \|w\|.
    \]
    Then \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn} implies that $\|R M P - R_{\mathbb{Q}} M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}\| \leq 3 \kappa (1 + \kappa)^3$ and the statement follows because $(1 + \kappa)^3 < 4/3$.
nodes.statement_short: Same with three factors.

nodes.name: Compare real and rational quantities
nodes.statement:
Let $G, H_{P}$ be the quantities in \cref{thm:global}. Then observe that 
    \[
        G \geq G^{\mathbb{Q}} \quad \text{ and } \quad H^{\mathbb{Q}}_P \geq H_P
    \]
    by \cref{lem:boundskappa}.
nodes.statement_short: The rational bounds give $G\ge G^\mathbb{Q}$, $H_P^\mathbb{Q}\ge H_P$.

nodes.name: Apply the Global Theorem
nodes.statement: It follows that, under the assumption of the theorem,  $G \geq G^{\mathbb{Q}} > \max_{P} H^{\mathbb{Q}}_P \geq  \max_{P} H_P$, thus we can apply \cref{thm:global} and conclude.
nodes.statement_short: The real hypothesis holds, so the Global Theorem applies.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
Set $M \coloneqq M(\theta, \varphi)$ and $M_{\mathbb{Q}} \coloneqq M_{\mathbb{Q}}(\theta, \varphi)$. It suffices to show that  
    \begin{align} | \langle R(\pi/2) M P_1,M P_{2}\rangle - \langle R(\pi/2) M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}_1,M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}_{2}\rangle| \leq 6 \kappa,
    \end{align}
    since then 
    \[
        \langle R(\pi/2) M P_1,M P_{2}\rangle \geq \langle R(\pi/2) M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}_1,M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}_{2}\rangle - 6\kappa > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon),
    \]
    analogously for the other two inequalities, and then \cref{lem:eps-spanning} concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to bound the real-rational difference by $6\kappa$.

nodes.name: Product bound
nodes.statement:
To see that inequality (\ref{eq:Rpi/2kappa}) holds true, note that the left-hand side can be written as 
    \[
        | P_2^t M^t R(\pi/2) M P_1 - \widetilde{P}^t_{2} M^t_{\mathbb{Q}} R(\pi/2) M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}_1|, 
    \]
    which is bounded by $5 \kappa (1 + \kappa)^4 \leq 6\kappa$ with \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn}.
nodes.statement_short: Write as a matrix product and apply the product approximation bound.

nodes.name: Bound (1)
nodes.statement: Note that if $\|P\| \leq 1$ then $\|\widetilde{P}\| \leq 1 + \kappa$. Rewrite (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.1}) as $ | P^t X - \widetilde{P}^t X_{\mathbb{Q}} | $ and then observe that \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn} yields the bound $2 \kappa (1 + \kappa)^2 \leq 3\kappa$.
nodes.statement_short: Product bound for $P^tX$.

nodes.name: Bound (2)
nodes.statement: Inequality (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.3}) follows in a similar way by rewriting the left-hand side as $| Q^t M^t MP -  \widetilde{Q}^t M_{\mathbb{Q}}^t M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P} |$, applying \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn} and using that $4 \kappa (1+\kappa)^4 \leq 5\kappa$.
nodes.statement_short: Product bound for $Q^tM^tMP$.

nodes.name: Bound (3)
nodes.statement: Finally for (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.2}), observe that by the reverse triangle inequality it holds that $|\| M Q \| - \| M_{\mathbb{Q}}\widetilde{Q} \| |\leq \| MQ - M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{Q} \| $ and the latter is bounded by $2 \kappa (1 + \kappa)^2 \leq  3\kappa$ using \cref{lem:A1AnB1Bn}.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse triangle inequality and product bound.

nodes.name: Numerator scalar product
nodes.statement:
Note that $(\widetilde{P}-\widetilde{Q})/2$ is a $\kappa$-rational approximation of $(P-Q)/2$ and that $\|(P-Q)/2\| \leq 1$. Therefore, by \cref{lem:boundskappa3}'s inequality (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.3}) it holds that 
    \[
       \bigg| \Big \langle M P, M \frac{P-Q}{2} \Big \rangle - \Big \langle M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}, M_{\mathbb{Q}} \frac{\widetilde{P}-\widetilde{Q}}{2} \Big \rangle \bigg | \leq  5\kappa,
    \]
    and consequently we obtain that 
    \[
        \langle M P, M (P-Q) \rangle \geq \langle M P, M (\widetilde{P}-\widetilde{Q}) \rangle - 10\kappa.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the rational local bound to $(P-Q)/2$.

nodes.name: Numerator comparison
nodes.statement:
Further, the triangle inequality implies that 
    \[
        \|P-Q\| \leq \|\widetilde{P}-\widetilde{Q}\| + 2 \kappa \leq \|\widetilde{P}-\widetilde{Q}\|_{+} + 2 \kappa.
    \]
    It follows that the numerator of $A_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is at most the numerator of $A$ and that both are positive.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|P-Q\|$ and conclude the numerator comparison.

nodes.name: Denominator comparison
nodes.statement:
Finally, (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.2}) implies that 
    \[
        \| M P\| \leq \| M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}\| + 3\kappa \leq \|  M_{\mathbb{Q}} \widetilde{P}\|_{+} + 3\kappa, 
    \]
    and also that 
    \[
        \| M (P-Q)\| = 2\Big \| M \frac{P-Q}{2} \Big\| \leq 2 \Big \| M_{\mathbb{Q}} \frac{\widetilde{P} - \widetilde{Q}}{2} \Big\| + 6\kappa \leq \|  M_{\mathbb{Q}} (\widetilde{P} - \widetilde{Q})\|_{+} + 6\kappa.
    \]
    Therefore, the denominator of $A$ is at most the denominator of $A_{\mathbb{Q}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound both denominator factors.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We shall show that we may apply \cref{thm:local}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Local Theorem.

nodes.name: Condition (A)
nodes.statement: The inequalities in (A$^{\mathbb{Q}}_\varepsilon$) imply (A$_\varepsilon$) thanks to (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.1}) in \cref{lem:boundskappa3}.
nodes.statement_short: Rational (A) implies real (A).

nodes.name: Condition (B)
nodes.statement: Similarly, (B$^{\mathbb{Q}}_\varepsilon$) implies (B$_\varepsilon$) by \cref{lem:boundskappa4}. Note that the bound on $r$ uses (\ref{eq:boundskappa3.2}) and the bound for $\delta$ uses \cref{corr:deltakappa}.
nodes.statement_short: Rational (B) implies real (B), with bounds for $r$ and $\delta$.

nodes.name: Spanning conditions
nodes.statement: The assumption that $\widetilde{P}_1,\widetilde{P}_2,\widetilde{P}_3$ are $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning implies that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are $\varepsilon$-spanning by \cref{lem:ekspanningespanning}, and analogously for $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning implies $\varepsilon$-spanning.

nodes.name: Explicit solution
nodes.statement:
A solution for $\mathbf{RUP}$ can be found using the methods described in \cite{StYu23}. Specifically, it can be checked using a computer algebra software that
    \[
        (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)=(0.29,0.29,0.02,2.27,-1.02)
    \]
    is a solution for $\mathbf{RUP}$'s Rupert's property and that it has Nieuwland number greater than $1.003$. This proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: An explicit parameter tuple, checked by computer algebra, proves part (1).

nodes.name: Cover local parameters by cubes
nodes.statement:
Using the same symmetries described in \cref{lem:symmetries}, it is clear that we can assume $\theta_1\in[0,2\pi/15], \varphi_1\in[0,\pi/2]$ and $\alpha \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.
    We define the sequence of points $A_k \coloneqq \omega\cdot k \in \mathbb{R}$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Note, that $A_{699}>2\pi/15$ and $A_{2618}>\pi/2$. We further define the five-dimensional closed cubes $B_{i,j}\subset \mathbb{R}^5$ for $i=0,\dots,699$, $j=0,\dots, 2618$ by
    \[
        B_{i,j} \coloneqq [A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, 0\pm\omega].
    \]
    If a solution $\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)$ would exist as stated in (2) then, for some $0\leq i\leq 699$ and some $0\leq j\leq 2618$, it would hold that $\Psi \in B_{i,j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce by symmetry and cover the local parameter set by cubes $B_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Symmetry reduction
nodes.statement: Using the same symmetries described in \cref{lem:symmetries}, it is clear that we can assume $\theta_1\in[0,2\pi/15], \varphi_1\in[0,\pi/2]$ and $\alpha \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.
nodes.statement_short: The NOP-style symmetries reduce the ranges.

nodes.name: Grid of cubes
nodes.statement:
We define the sequence of points $A_k \coloneqq \omega\cdot k \in \mathbb{R}$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Note, that $A_{699}>2\pi/15$ and $A_{2618}>\pi/2$. We further define the five-dimensional closed cubes $B_{i,j}\subset \mathbb{R}^5$ for $i=0,\dots,699$, $j=0,\dots, 2618$ by
    \[
        B_{i,j} \coloneqq [A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, A_i\pm\omega, A_j\pm\omega, 0\pm\omega].
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $A_k=\omega k$ and cubes $B_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Covering
nodes.statement: If a solution $\Psi = (\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)$ would exist as stated in (2) then, for some $0\leq i\leq 699$ and some $0\leq j\leq 2618$, it would hold that $\Psi \in B_{i,j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any local solution lies in some $B_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Exclude each region
nodes.statement: However, similarly to the solution tree for \cref{thm:main}, we can construct regions $C_k\subset \mathbb{R}^5$ for $0\leq k \leq 3534$ such that each $B_{i,j}$ is a subset of at least one $C_k$, and such that it is possible to prove using the rational local \cref{thm:local_rational} that there does not exist a solution $\Psi \in C_k$ for all $k$. The definition of $(C_k)_{0 \leq k \leq 3534}$, the list which $B_{i,j}$  lies within which $C_k$ and the verification code are stored on \href{https://github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}{www.github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}.
nodes.statement_short: Regions $C_k$ covering all $B_{i,j}$ are each excluded with the rational local theorem by computer.

nodes.name: Strategy: solution tree
nodes.statement:
In \cref{cor:NOPbounds} of \cref{sec:noperthedron} we have proven that if $\mathbf{NOP}$ was Rupert then there would exists a solution to its Rupert's condition (\ref{eq:rupert_condition}) with  
\begin{align*}    
\theta_1,\theta_2&\in[0,2\pi/15] \subset [0,0.42], \\
\varphi_1&\in [0,\pi] \subset [0,3.15],\\
\varphi_2&\in [0,\pi/2] \subset [0,1.58],\\
\alpha &\in [-\pi/2,\pi/2] \subset [-1.58,1.58].
\end{align*}

Generally speaking, in order to prove that a solution for any solid $\mathbf{P}$ does not exist within any given five dimensional interval for $[\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1, \overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2, \overline{\alpha}] \pm \varepsilon \subseteq \mathbb{R}^5$, we can establish 3 (recursive) options:
\begin{itemize}
    \item [(I)] Apply the (rational) global theorem (\cref{thm:global}),
    \item [(II)] Apply the (rational) local theorem (\cref{thm:local}),
    \item [(III)] Subdivide the interval into smaller intervals, and for each of them again apply one of (I)--(III).
\end{itemize}

To show that the Noperthedron is not Rupert, one can now think of creating a ``solution tree'' with each node corresponding to some interval and the root of the tree representing the initial interval from \cref{cor:NOPbounds}. 
If a node/interval can be proven to not contain a solution (using the global or the local theorems) then this node is a leaf. Otherwise, one might write the interval as a union of smaller intervals, each of which is then one of its children.

For $\mathbf{NOP}$ we have created such a tree algorithmically in the programming language \href{https://www.r-project.org/}{R} using floating point operations. 
On a good PC this took roughly 7 hours and used less than 4 GB of RAM. This tree has 585\,200 interior nodes and 18\,115\,245 leaf nodes, 17\,492\,530 of which can be solved using the global theorem and 622\,715 of which using the local theorem. It is stored in the form of a tabular database such that each of its rows corresponds to one node. Additionally, we store information about how the rational global/local theorems can be applied. 
The generation code and solution file can be found in \href{https://github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}{www.github.com/Jakob256/Rupert} with an excerpt of the latter displayed in \cref{tab:solution_tree} below. In \cref{sec:structure} we explain more details about the  structure of the solution tree.

Note that the floating point driven \href{https://www.r-project.org/}{R} code is not part of the proof of \cref{thm:main}: The algorithmic rigorous verification of the solution tree was programmed in \href{https://www.sagemath.org/}{SageMath}. This code checks that the rational versions of the global and local theorems can be applied to each leaf and that the union of them is the initial interval. This step is computationally more expensive and takes about 30 hours on the same PC. In \cref{sec:verification} we explain this code which is available on \href{https://github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}{www.github.com/Jakob256/Rupert}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the reduced box and describe the solution tree built in R and verified in SageMath.

nodes.name: Structure of the solution tree
nodes.statement:
As mentioned above, our tabular solution tree for the Noperthedron contains all necessary information needed for proving that this solid does not have Rupert's property. Each of its rows corresponds to a five-dimensional interval for a possible solution $(\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)$ with an indication which of the three options above (I), (II), (III) to apply. In the subdivision case (III) the data in the row points to the children of the node and in the cases (I) and (II) the row contains information on how to apply the global or local theorems to the interval. 
More precisely, the table has the following~columns:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{ID}: Is a unique consecutive number for each row.
    \item \textbf{nodeType}: A number 1, 2 or 3, corresponding to the options (I), (II) or (III) above. 
    \item \textbf{nrChildren}: In the subdivision case (nodeType=3), the number of children this node has.
    \item \textbf{IDfirstChild}: In the case nodeType=3, the ID of the first child node. The children are stored as consequentive rows, therefore nrChildren and IDfirstChild are enough to recover~them. 
    \item \textbf{split}: When nodeType=3, for convenience, we store a variable which records how the interval is going to be split. There are the following options:
    \begin{align*}
        \text{split} =1 & \iff \text{only the interval for } \overline{\theta}_1 \text{ is split},\\
        \text{split} =2 & \iff \text{only the interval for } \overline{\varphi}_1 \text{ is split},\\
        \text{split} =3 & \iff \text{only the interval for } \overline{\theta}_2 \text{ is split},\\
        \text{split} =4 & \iff \text{only the interval for } \overline{\varphi}_2 \text{ is split},\\
        \text{split} =5 & \iff \text{only the interval for } \overline{\alpha} \text{ is split},\\
        \text{split} =6 & \iff \text{all five intervals are split in half}.
    \end{align*}
    In other words, for $\mathrm{split} \in \{1,\dots,5\}$ the corresponding interval is divided in nrChildren equal parts, whereas if $\mathrm{split}=6$ then all intervals are halved resulting in $\mathrm{nrChildren}=2^5 = 32$. 
    \item \textbf{T1\_min}, \textbf{T1\_max}, \textbf{V1\_min}, \textbf{V1\_max}, \textbf{T2\_min}, \textbf{T2\_max}, \textbf{V2\_min}, \textbf{V2\_max}, \textbf{A\_min}, \textbf{A\_max} are the numerators of the boundaries for the interval of the node/row:
    \begin{align*}
        N \cdot \theta_1 & \in [T1_{\min}, T1_{\max} ], \\ 
        N \cdot\varphi_1 & \in [V1_{\min}, V1_{\max} ], \\
        N \cdot\theta_2 & \in [T2_{\min}, T2_{\max} ], \\ 
        N \cdot\varphi_2 & \in [V2_{\min}, V2_{\max} ], \\ 
        N \cdot\alpha & \in [A_{\min}, A_{\max} ],
    \end{align*}
    with $N$ set to 15\,360\,000.
    \item \textbf{S\_index}: The index of the vertex $S$ for applying the (rational) global theorem (\cref{thm:global_rational}), used if nodeType=1.
    \item \textbf{wx\_nominator}, \textbf{wy\_nominator}, \textbf{w\_denominator} are the numerators and common denominator of the components of the unit vector $w = (w_x, w_y) \in \mathbb{Q}^2$ in \cref{thm:global_rational} (present if nodeType=1).
    \item \textbf{P1\_index}, \textbf{P2\_index}, \textbf{P3\_index}, \textbf{Q1\_index}, \textbf{Q2\_index}, \textbf{Q3\_index}: The indices of the congruent triples $P_1,P_2,P_3,Q_1,Q_2,Q_3 \in \mathbf{NOP}$ from \cref{thm:local_rational}, used if nodeType=2.
    \item \textbf{r}, \textbf{sigma\_Q}: The numerator $r'$ of the rational number $r = r'/1000 \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $\sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$ from \cref{thm:local_rational} (if nodeType=2).
\end{enumerate}

Note that all entries of the table are integers, therefore no rounding loss occurs when loading or storing it. 
When talking about \textit{indices of vertices} we refer to the ordering $\mathbf{NOP} = (P_0, \dots, P_{89})$ defined as
\begin{align} P_{k+15i+45 \ell}=(-1)^\ell R_z\left(\frac{2\pi k}{15}\right)C_{i+1}
\quad \text{ for } \quad i \in \{0,1,2\}, \; k \in \{0,\dots,14\}, \; \ell \in \{0,1\},
\end{align}
and $C_1, C_2, C_3 \in \mathbb{Q}^3$ given in \cref{sec:noperthedron}. Moreover, we always assume that $\sigma_{P} = 0$, so we only store~$\sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$.

Each of its rows corresponds to a five-dimensional interval for a possible solution $(\theta_1, \varphi_1, \theta_2, \varphi_2, \alpha)$ with an indication which of the three options above (I), (II), (III) to apply. In the subdivision case (III) the data in the row points to the children of the node and in the cases (I) and (II) the row contains information on how to apply the global or local theorems to the interval.

nodes.name: Verification
nodes.statement:
In order to verify that the solution tree indeed proves \cref{thm:main} we must check the following assertions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(A)] The union of all leaf intervals (rows with nodeType=1 or 2) contains the interval in \cref{cor:NOPbounds},
    \item[(B)] For each row with nodeType=1 one can apply \cref{thm:global_rational} and for each row with nodeType=2 one can apply \cref{thm:local_rational}.
\end{enumerate}

In order to check (A) we first verify that for each node the union of all its children contains its interval. Further we check that all nodes are either leafs (nodeType=1 or 2) or interval nodes (nodeType=3), and that the root contains the interval in \cref{cor:NOPbounds}. With the fact that the ID of any child is always strictly larger than the ID of the parent, this proves (A).

The verification of (B) splits into two cases: nodeType=1 or nodeType=2. They are explained in \cref{sec:veriglob} and \cref{sec:veriloc}. For each of them $\widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}}$ is defined as the following truncation of all vertices of $\mathbf{NOP}$ to 16 decimal places and is therefore a $\kappa$-rational approximation:
\[
    \widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}} \coloneqq \lfloor10^{16} \cdot \mathbf{NOP} \rfloor /10^{16}.
\]
The indices correspond to points via the ordering in (\ref{eq:ordering}). Both cases start with the following two operations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Set $N=15\,360\,000$ and compute 
    \begin{align*}
    \overline{\theta}_1 & = (T1_{\min} + T1_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\varphi}_1 & = (V1_{\min} + V1_{\max} )/(2N), \\
    \overline{\theta}_2 & = (T2_{\min} + T2_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\varphi}_2 & = (V2_{\min} + V2_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\alpha} & = (A_{\min} + A_{\max} )/(2N).
\end{align*}
Check that $\overline{\theta}_i, \overline{\varphi}_i, \overline{\alpha} \in [-4,4]$.
\item Set $\varepsilon = \max(T1_{\max} - T1_{\min}, V1_{\max} - V1_{\min},T2_{\max} - T2_{\min}, V1_{\max} - V1_{\min}, A_{\max} - A_{\min})/(2N)$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Verification of the global theorem} The verification of the rational global theorem (\cref{thm:global_rational}) is relatively straightforward. Namely, for every row in the solution tree which has noteType=1 we must perform the following operations (additionally to 1. and 2. above):
\begin{enumerate}
    \setcounter{enumi}{2}
    \item Set $w = ($wx\_numerator/w\_denominator, wy\_numerator/w\_denominator$) \in \mathbb{Q}^2$ and check that $\|w\|^2 = w_1^2 + w_2^2=1$.
    \item Set $\widetilde{S}$ to be the rationally approximated point corresponding to the index given in column~S\_index.
    \item Compute $\overline{M_1}$, $\overline{M_2}$, $\overline{M_1}^\theta$, $\overline{M_1}^\varphi$, $\overline{M_2}^\theta$, $\overline{M_2}^\varphi \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 3}$ and $R_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}), R'_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}) \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 2}$ as in \cref{thm:global_rational}.
    \item Compute $G^{\mathbb{Q}} \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $H_{P}^{\mathbb{Q}} \in \mathbb{Q}$ for all $P \in \widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}}$ as in \cref{thm:global_rational}.
    \item Verify that $G^{\mathbb{Q}} > \max H_{P}^{\mathbb{Q}}$.
\end{enumerate}

Note that all steps only use rational numbers, thus in the computer algebra system \href{https://www.sagemath.org/}{SageMath} no rounding loss or precision errors can occur.

\subsubsection{Verification of the local theorem} For the verification of the rational local \cref{thm:local_rational} for all rows of the solution tree with nodeType=2 we have to perform more work.

First, recall that in \cref{def:sqrtplusminus} and \cref{thm:local_rational} we define/use the upper- and lower-square root functions $\sqrt[+]{x}, \sqrt[-]{x} \colon \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}$ given via
    \[
        \sqrt[-]{x} \leq \sqrt{x} \leq \sqrt[+]{x}.
    \]
    We decided to implement the following functions since they allow a precise control on the size of the denominator/accuracy and at the same time can be relatively efficiently implemented: 
    
    First, set $\sqrt[-]{0}=\sqrt[+]{0}=0$. For any $x>0$, there exists a unique $a\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that 
    \[
        x \cdot 10^{2a}\in [10^{20},10^{22}),
    \]
    and then there exists a unique $b\in \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that 
    \[
        b^2\leq x\cdot 10^{2a} < (b+1)^2.
    \]
    Observe that $b/10^a \leq \sqrt{x}$, so we define 
    \begin{align} \sqrt[-]{x} \coloneqq \frac{b}{10^a} \quad \text{and} \quad \sqrt[+]{x} \coloneqq \frac{1}{\sqrt[-]{1/x}}.
    \end{align}
    We then also define 
    \[
        \|Z\|_{-} \coloneqq \sqrt[-]{\|Z\|^2} \quad \text{ and } \quad \|Z\|_{+} \coloneqq \sqrt[+]{\|Z\|^2}
    \]
    for any $Z \in \mathbb{Q}^{n}$, so that $\|Z\|_{-},\|Z\|_{+} \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $\|Z\|_{-} \leq \|Z\| \leq \|Z\|_{+}$. \\

    Similarly to the global theorem verification after the steps 1. and 2. above, we perform the following steps for each row with nodeType=2:

    \begin{enumerate}
    \setcounter{enumi}{2}
    \item Check that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ and $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are congruent by applying \cref{lem:congruent} (verifying that $P^tP = Q^tQ$ and $\det(Q) \neq 0$).
    \item Compute $\overline{M_1}$, $\overline{M_2} \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 3}$, $\overline{X_1}, \overline{X_2} \in \mathbb{Q}^{3}$ and $R_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}) \in \mathbb{Q}^{2 \times 2}$ as in \cref{thm:global_rational}.
    \item Set $\sigma_Q =$ sigma\_Q and check that 
    \[
        \langle \overline{X_1}, \widetilde{P}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon + 3 \kappa \quad \text{ and } \quad (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2},\widetilde{P}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon +3 \kappa.
    \]
    \item Check that $\widetilde{P}_1,\widetilde{P}_2,\widetilde{P}_3$ are $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $\widetilde{Q}_1,\widetilde{Q}_2,\widetilde{Q}_3$ are $\varepsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)$ by verifying the inequalities in \cref{def:ekspanning}:
        \begin{align*}
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_1, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{2}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_2, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{3}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_3, \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_{1}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,
        \end{align*}
        and 
            \begin{align*}
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_1, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{2}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_2, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{3}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa,\\
                \langle R(\pi/2) \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_3, \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_{1}\rangle > 2 \varepsilon(\sqrt{2} + \varepsilon) + 6\kappa.
        \end{align*}
    \item Set $r = r'/1000 \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r'$ taken from the r column and define
        \[
            \delta = \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1} \widetilde{P}_i-\overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i\right\|_{+}/2 + 3\kappa \in \mathbb{Q}.
        \]
    \item Check that $\| \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i \|_{-} > r + \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 3\kappa$ for $i=1,2,3$.
    \item Finally verify that 
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i,\overline{M_2} (\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\rangle - 10\kappa - 2 \varepsilon ( \|\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j\|_{+} + 2 \kappa ) \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2} \widetilde{Q}_i\|_{+}+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 3\kappa \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\|_{+}+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 6 \kappa\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \varepsilon + \delta}{r},
    \]
    for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $\widetilde{Q}_j \in \widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}} \setminus \widetilde{Q}_i$.
\end{enumerate}

Note that $\sqrt{2}$ in the steps 5., 6., 8. and 9. can be approximated by $142/100 = 1.42 > \sqrt{2}$ making the inequalities stricter and the expressions rational. Similarly, we approximate $\sqrt{5}$ in step 9. by $224/100 = 2.24 > \sqrt{5}$, so that also this condition becomes a statement on purely rational numbers. It follows that the only non-rational condition to check is step 3., namely that 
\(
P^tP = Q^tQ
\)
for $P = (P_1|P_2|P_3) \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^{3 \times 3}$, $Q = (Q_1|Q_2|Q_3)\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^{3 \times 3}$ and that $\det(Q) \neq 0$. Note that these expressions are, however, over algebraic numbers and \href{https://www.sagemath.org/}{SageMath} can prove them relatively~quickly. 

\bigskip

We implemented the verification of the solution tree integrity as well as the procedures of \cref{sec:veriglob} and \cref{sec:veriloc} in \href{https://www.sagemath.org/}{SageMath}. The total run time of this code is roughly 30h on a good PC which roughly consists of 1h for the solution tree integrity check, 16h of verification of rational global theorems and 10h of rational local theorems verification. 
This finally finishes the proof of \cref{thm:main}.

For each of them $\widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}}$ is defined as the following truncation of all vertices of $\mathbf{NOP}$ to 16 decimal places and is therefore a $\kappa$-rational approximation:
\[
    \widetilde{\mathbf{NOP}} \coloneqq \lfloor10^{16} \cdot \mathbf{NOP} \rfloor /10^{16}.
\]
The indices correspond to points via the ordering in (\ref{eq:ordering}). Both cases start with the following two operations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Set $N=15\,360\,000$ and compute 
    \begin{align*}
    \overline{\theta}_1 & = (T1_{\min} + T1_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\varphi}_1 & = (V1_{\min} + V1_{\max} )/(2N), \\
    \overline{\theta}_2 & = (T2_{\min} + T2_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\varphi}_2 & = (V2_{\min} + V2_{\max} )/(2N), \\ 
    \overline{\alpha} & = (A_{\min} + A_{\max} )/(2N).
\end{align*}
Check that $\overline{\theta}_i, \overline{\varphi}_i, \overline{\alpha} \in [-4,4]$.
\item Set $\varepsilon = \max(T1_{\max} - T1_{\min}, V1_{\max} - V1_{\min},T2_{\max} - T2_{\min}, V1_{\max} - V1_{\min}, A_{\max} - A_{\min})/(2N)$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Truncate NOP to 16 decimals and compute midpoints and $\varepsilon$ for each leaf.

nodes.name: Local leaves: recall square roots
nodes.statement:
For the verification of the rational local \cref{thm:local_rational} for all rows of the solution tree with nodeType=2 we have to perform more work.

First, recall that in \cref{def:sqrtplusminus} and \cref{thm:local_rational} we define/use the upper- and lower-square root functions $\sqrt[+]{x}, \sqrt[-]{x} \colon \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}$ given via
    \[
        \sqrt[-]{x} \leq \sqrt{x} \leq \sqrt[+]{x}.
    \]
nodes.statement_short: Local leaves need upper and lower rational square roots.
nodes.section: 7 The algorithmic part of the proof

nodes.name: Implemented square roots
nodes.statement:
We decided to implement the following functions since they allow a precise control on the size of the denominator/accuracy and at the same time can be relatively efficiently implemented: 
    
    First, set $\sqrt[-]{0}=\sqrt[+]{0}=0$. For any $x>0$, there exists a unique $a\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that 
    \[
        x \cdot 10^{2a}\in [10^{20},10^{22}),
    \]
    and then there exists a unique $b\in \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that 
    \[
        b^2\leq x\cdot 10^{2a} < (b+1)^2.
    \]
    Observe that $b/10^a \leq \sqrt{x}$, so we define 
    \begin{align} \sqrt[-]{x} \coloneqq \frac{b}{10^a} \quad \text{and} \quad \sqrt[+]{x} \coloneqq \frac{1}{\sqrt[-]{1/x}}.
    \end{align}
    We then also define 
    \[
        \|Z\|_{-} \coloneqq \sqrt[-]{\|Z\|^2} \quad \text{ and } \quad \|Z\|_{+} \coloneqq \sqrt[+]{\|Z\|^2}
    \]
    for any $Z \in \mathbb{Q}^{n}$, so that $\|Z\|_{-},\|Z\|_{+} \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $\|Z\|_{-} \leq \|Z\| \leq \|Z\|_{+}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\sqrt[\pm]{x}$ via integer square roots at 10-11 significant digits.
